heading: Issues of Edward's age
summary: Edward's minority created serious concerns about faction, regency and the stability of government.
facts: Henry VIII had issued his Third Act of Succession in 1543, confirming that if Edward died without children the throne would pass to Mary and then Elizabeth. The religious and factional struggles of Henry's latter years had left the Council divided between reformists and conservatives. Henry's death left these tensions unresolved.

When Edward became King in January 1547 aged nine there were serious concerns: he would not be able to lead troops into battle; a regent might seize power as had happened in previous minorities; he would be unable to control faction; and the image of monarchy as a strong, divine power would be challenged by the image of a child.

However not all previous minorities had ended badly. Edward was not a sickly child and his succession had been expected. He was noted as an extremely bright boy who showed great promise as a ruler — and by 1552-53 he was taking a far more active role in government aged 14-15.

Henry had tried to prevent the dangers of a single regent by instructing that a Regency Council of 16 co-equal members be formed, balanced between reformists such as Seymour and conservatives led by Gardiner and Norfolk. However the fall from grace of Gardiner and Norfolk in 1546 left the Council weighted in favour of the reformists.

Following Henry's death, Somerset and Paget conspired using the dry stamp and the 'unfulfilled gifts' clause of Henry's will to increase their power. Somerset was made Duke of Somerset, Lord Protector and predominant figure on the new Regency Council — going directly against Henry's wishes for 16 co-equal members.

Somerset's rise was initially unopposed. As Edward's uncle and a successful general, it was not surprising. However some questioned the legality as it went against Henry's will — a sign that the factional divisions that would destabilise Edward's reign were already present.

heading: The Regency Council
summary: Somerset used his position as Lord Protector to accumulate power, creating the factional tensions that would lead to his fall.
facts: Henry had instructed that a Regency Council of 16 members be formed — balanced between reformists such as Seymour and conservatives led by Gardiner and Norfolk. However Gardiner and Norfolk's fall from grace in 1546 meant the Council was already weighted in favour of the reformists before Henry died.

Following Henry's death, Somerset and Paget conspired using the dry stamp (a method of authenticating documents without the King's signature) and the 'unfulfilled gifts' clause of Henry's will to increase their own wealth and power. Somerset was made Duke of Somerset, Lord Protector and predominant figure on the new Regency Council.

As Lord Protector Somerset was able to use his position to increase his personal wealth and power, which resulted in criticism from opponents and even former supporters. Somerset's arrogant and dominating leadership created a new faction: the Anti-Somerset faction — a combination of reformers and conservatives who all hated Somerset, including Warwick, Wriothesley and Paget.

The Anti-Somerset faction feared Somerset's apparent sympathy for the commoners and the problem of enclosure — they believed this sympathy had encouraged the unrest of the summer of 1549. Edward himself disliked Somerset's control as he was allowed no influence at all.

The unrest of 1549 weakened Somerset's hold on power as many in the Council blamed his policies. Feeling threatened, Somerset took possession of Edward and issued a general summons for all loyal subjects to defend the King. On the 6th October Somerset retreated to Windsor Castle but was forced to surrender to the Council when the King turned against him. Somerset was arrested.

subheadings.label: Henry's intentions
facts: Faction in government is not inevitably a destabilising force for monarchs. Other Tudor monarchs encouraged faction to ensure their ministers competed for their loyalty.
However, faction in the reign of a minor was more dangerous as there was no authority to control it. Factional disputes could spill over into rebellion or civil war.

heading: The rise of Northumberland
summary: Northumberland filled the power vacuum after Somerset's fall, securing his position by allying with the reformists and fabricating charges against Somerset.
facts: Following Somerset's fall there was a power vacuum on the Regency Council. Warwick's role in the defeat of both the Western and Kett's rebellions had made him politically indispensable — he was seen as a strong leader who could restore order.

Facing opposition from conservatives including the Earls of Arundel and Southampton, Warwick allied himself with the reformist faction and committed to further religious reform — becoming Lord President of the Council in 1550 and Duke of Northumberland.

He released Somerset and restored him to the Council in the hope he would use his influence to stabilise the regime — but when this failed, Somerset was arrested again and executed for treason in January 1552.
The evidence suggests the accusations of treason against Somerset were fabricated — Northumberland needed to remove the one figure who could plausibly challenge his dominance of the Council.

Northumberland's methods showed how dangerous minority rule was — without a strong monarch, the most ruthless faction could dominate government and eliminate opponents under cover of law. Edward himself was becoming more active in government by 1552–53, aged 14–15.

Northumberland promoted rapid Protestant reform under Stage 3 — the Second Book of Common Prayer (1552) and Forty-Two Articles — partly out of genuine conviction but also to cement his alliance with the reformist faction.

heading: The Devise for the Succession
summary: Edward and Northumberland attempted to exclude Mary from the succession by naming Lady Jane Grey as heir, but Mary's popular support ensured her triumph.
facts: Henry VIII had stipulated in the Third Act of Succession that if Edward died without children the throne would pass to Mary Tudor. In early 1553 Edward VI's health began to decline causing anxiety about this line of succession.

Edward himself was concerned for the survival of the radical Protestant changes he valued. Mary was a committed Catholic who had maintained her faith throughout Edward's reign — even Edward's personal appeals could not move her. Mary's accession would lead to the restoration of Catholicism.

Northumberland was concerned for his own power — he knew his role under Edward would lead to his fall from power when Mary came to the throne. There is debate about who was more responsible in developing the Devise — Edward was 15 and taking a far more active role in government by 1553.

The 'Devise for the Succession' was written naming the future male children of Jane Grey as Edward's heirs. To preserve his power, Northumberland married his son Guildford Dudley to Jane Grey. However Edward's illness progressed rapidly. In his own hand Edward crossed out the phrase 'male heirs' and named Jane Grey herself as his heir.

Edward died on 6th July 1553. His death was kept quiet for two days whilst prominent nobles were pressured to sign the Devise. Mary acted quickly — she had a significant power base in East Anglia and quickly dispatched riders to proclaim herself Queen, calling for support from loyal subjects and her cousin Charles V, Holy Roman Emperor.

The Council proclaimed Jane as Queen on the 10th July, after Mary's proclamation on the 9th. Northumberland left London to face Mary but many of his army deserted him and Councillors broke ranks and declared support for Mary. Northumberland retreated to Cambridge and accepted Mary was Queen on the 19th. Mary had Northumberland, Lady Jane Grey and Guildford Dudley arrested and later executed.

heading: The Lady Jane Grey affair
summary: The Lady Jane Grey affair of July 1553 was the most direct challenge to the legitimate succession since Henry VIII's reign — and its rapid failure revealed the limits of Northumberland's power.
facts: The Lady Jane Grey affair grew directly out of the Devise for the Succession. Edward VI and Northumberland feared that Mary's accession would mean the restoration of Catholicism and the end of Northumberland's power. The Devise named Jane Grey — a Protestant great-niece of Henry VIII — as Edward's heir, bypassing both Mary and Elizabeth.

Northumberland strengthened his grip by marrying Jane to his son Guildford Dudley in May 1553. When Edward died on 6th July 1553, his death was kept secret for two days whilst prominent nobles were pressured to sign the Devise. The Council then proclaimed Jane as Queen on 10th July.

Mary acted immediately and decisively. She had a significant power base in East Anglia and quickly dispatched riders to proclaim herself Queen, calling for support from loyal subjects and her cousin Charles V, Holy Roman Emperor. Many of the gentry and nobility rallied to Mary — not necessarily out of Catholic sympathy but out of respect for legitimate hereditary succession.

Northumberland left London to face Mary with an army but many of his troops deserted him. Councillors who had been forced to sign the Devise broke ranks and declared for Mary. Northumberland retreated to Cambridge and accepted Mary was Queen on 19th July 1553. The affair had lasted just nine days.

Why it failed: the Devise had no legal basis and went against Henry VIII's Third Act of Succession. Most people believed in hereditary succession as divinely ordained. Mary's gender was seen as less important than the principle of legitimate succession. Northumberland had overreached — he lacked the popular support that Somerset had at least initially enjoyed.

Consequences: Northumberland, Lady Jane Grey and Guildford Dudley were all executed. Mary released Gardiner and Norfolk from jail and showed leniency towards many who had opposed her — demonstrating political judgement. The failure of the Devise showed that attempts to manipulate the succession without popular or noble backing were doomed.

heading: Issues of Mary's gender
summary: Mary's accession as the first Queen regnant raised deep concerns about female rule, though the willingness to make Jane Grey queen shows religion mattered more than gender.
facts: Mary was the first Queen to rule England in her own right. In the 12th century Matilda had been named heir but following Henry I's death there was a civil war as many nobles refused to accept her. Henry VIII's determination to gain a male heir shows the anxieties of leaving the realm to a female ruler.

Many believed female rulers would not be able to: control powerful men in government; lead soldiers into battle; or display the power and strength that a monarch needed to epitomise. John Knox wrote The First Blast of the Trumpet Against the Monstrous Regiment of Women in 1558 comparing female rulers to 'the blind leading those who can see'. Radical Protestants viewed female rulers as unnatural.

However the willingness of Edward and Northumberland to make Jane Grey queen suggests issues of gender were seen as less important compared to religion. Mary herself demonstrated considerable strength and leadership during the Lady Jane Grey affair and the Guildhall speech during Wyatt's Rebellion.

Mary needed to marry to create an heir. Two major candidates emerged: Edward Courtenay, Earl of Devon, championed by Stephen Gardiner — a powerful English noble with royal blood who would secure Mary's reign; and Philip of Spain, championed by Paget and Mary's personal choice, who would bring powerful diplomatic alliances but risked a xenophobic popular reaction.

Fearing a negative reaction, a treaty was agreed: Philip would be named King but have no power in his own right; no Spaniards would be granted offices or lands in England; after Mary's death Philip would have no claim to the throne; England would not be entangled in Spain's wars. Despite reassurances, Wyatt's rebellion broke out in January 1554.

Ultimately the marriage ended unhappily. After Mary's phantom pregnancy, Philip rarely spent any time in England. When Mary died Philip commented he felt 'a reasonable regret'. The failure to produce an heir meant the Catholic restoration died with Mary.

heading: Mary's marriage
summary: Mary's marriage to Philip of Spain was carefully managed by treaty but ultimately ended unhappily, contributing to rebellion and foreign entanglement.
facts: Mary needed to marry to create an heir to ensure the longevity of her Catholic restoration. However, issues were raised about the suitor.

If Mary married an English noble this would lead to division and faction within court and Council. If Mary married a foreign prince this could lead to an unpopular influx of foreigners and England's entanglement in foreign wars.

Two major candidates emerged: Edward Courtenay, Earl of Devon, championed by Stephen Gardiner; and Philip of Spain, championed by Paget and Mary's personal choice. Philip would bring powerful diplomatic alliances as his father Charles V was Holy Roman Emperor and King of Spain. However, it risked a xenophobic popular reaction.

Fearing a negative reaction, a treaty was agreed by the Spanish representatives and Parliament to avoid instability. It was agreed that: Philip would be named King but have no power in his own right; no Spaniards would be granted offices or lands in England; after Mary's death Philip would have no claim to the throne; England would not be entangled in Spain's wars.
Despite reassurances, Wyatt's rebellion broke out in January 1554, ostensibly in reaction to the marriage to Philip.
Ultimately, the marriage ended unhappily. After Mary's phantom pregnancy, Philip rarely spent any time in England. When Mary died Philip commented he felt 'a reasonable regret'.

heading: Marian faction
summary: Mary streamlined her Council and dominated it through three key figures, though divisions between Gardiner and Pole over the pace of restoration created short-lived friction.
facts: One of the key criticisms of female rulers was that they would not be able to control the male ministers in their government, leading to damaging factional struggles. Mary was keen to ensure an efficient and streamlined administration: casual councillors were excluded from key committees in 1554; in 1555 Mary established an inner council so only her most valued advisors were present.

Mary's Council was dominated by three key figures: Stephen Gardiner, Bishop of Winchester — a committed Catholic who recognised the restoration of Catholicism would need careful action, cautious and persuasive by nature; William Paget — an eminent political survivor and exceptional administrator, not committed to religious change; Cardinal Reginald Pole — a fiercely zealous Catholic who had gone into exile under Henry VIII.

The Paget-Gardiner rivalry was the central factional conflict of Mary's reign. They divided over two issues: Mary's marriage and the pace of the Catholic restoration. Gardiner championed the English suitor Edward Courtenay, Earl of Devon; Paget championed Philip of Spain, knowing he was Mary's preferred choice and hoping to gain favour. Paget won this argument.

On religion, Gardiner and Pole were diametrically opposed. Gardiner stressed caution and persuasion — he opposed the heresy burnings as counter-productive and believed moderate Catholics should be accommodated. Pole favoured dramatic change backed by persecution. Gardiner's death in November 1555 ended his moderating influence; the burnings increased rapidly under Pole's direction from 1555 onwards.

Despite these divisions, for the majority of Mary's reign the Council worked effectively and carried out her wishes. The factional conflicts were far less destabilising than those of Edward's minority because Mary could exercise royal authority directly. Philip's departure in 1555 and Gardiner's death allowed Paget to dominate the Council — he was a capable administrator whose political survival instincts kept the Council functioning.

The factional conflict between Paget and Gardiner ultimately mattered less than the structural problem of Mary's reign — the failure to produce an heir. Factional disputes about the pace of religious change were resolved by death (Gardiner) and departure (Philip). The real crisis was dynastic, not factional.

heading: Succession in 1558
summary: Mary died having failed to produce an heir, leaving England weakened by debt and war, and Elizabeth faced an immediate Catholic challenge to her legitimacy.
facts: Mary died on 17th November 1558. Cardinal Pole died on the same day, leaving the Church of England without an Archbishop of Canterbury.
Mary had failed to produce an heir. Her phantom pregnancy in 1555 had raised hopes that were quickly dashed, and Philip had largely abandoned England after 1555.
England had also suffered the humiliation of losing Calais in 1558, the last English territory in France, as a consequence of Mary's decision to join Spain's war against France.

The succession passed peacefully to Elizabeth. Philip of Spain, despite having the power to press a claim, chose not to. He recognised Elizabeth as Queen, preferring a Protestant England to a France-aligned Catholic one.

However many Catholics viewed Elizabeth as illegitimate, due to the Pope's refusal to grant Henry VIII's divorce from Catherine of Aragon. Instead they believed Mary, Queen of Scots was the true Queen of England. Mary was a Catholic monarch, married to the French Dauphin Francis. King Henry II of France presented Mary as the true queen of England, a figure unifying Scotland, France and England against Elizabeth.
Elizabeth therefore inherited not just a country divided by religion, weakened by war and debt, but an immediate Catholic challenge to the legitimacy of her rule.

heading: Religious inheritance
summary: Henry VIII's Reformation was incomplete and ambiguous, leaving England with a divided Church and a population largely unfamiliar with Protestant doctrine.
facts: Despite Henry VIII's Break from Rome in 1534, Henry himself never truly embraced Protestantism — he only embraced Protestant changes that would bring him money and power, most notably the Dissolution of the Monasteries (1536-41). The 1539 Act of Six Articles confirmed Catholic doctrine including Transubstantiation, clerical celibacy, private masses and auricular confession.

The majority of the country, outside London and East Anglia, likely did not fully understand the differences between Catholicism and Protestantism and just wanted to worship as their ancestors had done for a millennium. The repeal of the Treason Act allowed radical Protestant preaching — Calvinism, Zwinglism and Lutheranism were all being preached, creating confusion about what the official doctrine actually was.

Henry left a divided Council — Gardiner and Norfolk's fall from grace in 1546 meant it was already weighted in favour of the reformists before Edward came to the throne, making further Protestant reform very likely. Somerset and Cranmer had been among Henry's reformist advisors and were now in a position to implement radical change.

The Dissolution of the Monasteries had removed a key source of Catholic charitable provision and community. But it had also created a powerful vested interest among the gentry who had bought monastic land — they would resist any Catholic restoration that threatened their property rights. This proved the greatest obstacle to Mary's restoration.

Evidence from people's wills shows little support for the Protestant changes except in London, the south-east and East Anglia — the areas closest to the centre of power. Many people simply conformed because they were told they had to. The rapid restoration of Catholicism under Mary might suggest that traditional religion still retained its popularity.

The repeal of the Treason Laws opened up a Pandora's Box of new radical ideas that the government could not control. Various versions of radical Protestantism were being preached. Whilst there was a vacuum of official doctrine from the Church of England, these preachers created confusion. The First Book of Common Prayer was Cranmer's attempt to fill this vacuum — though it did not please anyone.

heading: Edward's Reformation: destruction
summary: The first stage of the Edwardian Reformation in 1547 focused on dismantling the Catholic Church before a new settlement could be imposed.
facts: The leading architects of radical change, Archbishop Cranmer and Somerset, had to act slowly. Before they could install their new religion, the old had to be destroyed.
Royal injunctions were issued encouraging iconoclasm in churches across England.
Repeal of the Six Articles removed the Catholic doctrine set out by Henry.
Repeal of the Treason Act meant it was no longer treason to preach dissenting religious views.
Dissolution of the Chantries that were seen as superstitious forms of Catholic worship. Also brought in a lot of revenue and land for the Crown.

heading: Edward's Reformation: formulation
summary: The second and third stages of the Edwardian Reformation attempted to fill the religious vacuum with a new Protestant settlement, culminating in the explicitly Calvinist Second Book of Common Prayer.
facts: Stage 2 – Limbo, 1548–49: The repeal of the Treason Laws opened up a Pandora's Box of new radical ideas. Various versions of radical Protestantism were being preached including Calvinism, Zwinglism and Lutheranism.

In December 1548, Cranmer published his First Book of Common Prayer. This was enforced nationwide in the First Act of Uniformity. It was a compromise between the old and the new and did not please anyone. Notably it was extremely vague on the stance on Holy Communion. This Prayer Book prompted rebellion in the West Country.

Stage 3 – Formulation, 1550–53: Following Northumberland's rise the pace of religious reform increased. A new ordinal was introduced in 1550, allowing leading Catholic clergy to be deprived of their positions and replaced with Protestants.

In 1552, Cranmer published the Second Book of Common Prayer, enforced by the second Act of Uniformity. This was much more radical and unambiguous than the first. It removed all Catholic practices, and confirmed Calvin's doctrine that Communion was purely symbolic.
In 1552, the Forty-Two Articles, outlining the key doctrines of Edward's Church, were drawn up. Edward's death in 1553 ensured these Articles were never passed by Parliament.
Nevertheless, by 1553, de jure England was a Protestant country.

heading: De facto change under Edward
summary: Despite the legal changes, the Edwardian Reformation made limited impact on actual religious practice in most of England beyond London and the south-east.
facts: Just because de jure England was Protestant does not mean de facto this was true nationally. Edward's rule lasted six years — in an age when ideas spread slowly this was a small amount of time to upend 1,000 years of Catholic worship. The early caution showed by the government (e.g. Cranmer's First Book of Common Prayer) shows they anticipated opposition.

At a local level compliance was patchy and often superficial. Many parishes simply removed images and altars when required but continued private Catholic devotion. Evidence from people's wills shows little support for the Protestant changes except in London, the south-east and East Anglia. Many people simply conformed outwardly because they were told to — without any genuine conversion.

Clerical resistance and ignorance was a major obstacle. In his visitations around his diocese of Gloucester, Bishop Hooper reported that of 311 clergymen, 171 were unable to repeat the Ten Commandments and 40 could not find the Lord's Prayer. The government had been unable to train enough Protestant clergy to replace those who resisted change.

Popular opposition broke out most dramatically in the Western Rebellion of 1549 — led by clergy who objected to the First Book of Common Prayer. The rebels called the new service 'a Christmas game' because they could not understand the English. In Yorkshire, Hampshire and Oxfordshire there was also significant unrest with a religious dimension, though enclosure and economic grievances were mixed in.

There was little time for the more radical policies to have an impact. The Second Act of Uniformity and 42 Articles were only in the last months of Edward's reign. The repeated efforts to remove icons and conduct visitations prove the lack of uniformity — the changes were hard to enforce at parish level.

The rapid restoration of Catholicism under Mary might suggest that traditional religion still retained its popularity, particularly in the North and West. However it is equally possible that this simply reflects local willingness to conform to whatever the government required — the same passive obedience that had enabled the Edwardian reforms in the first place.

heading: Mary's religious aims
summary: Mary aimed to restore England to full Papal authority and Catholic practice, though her advisors cautioned against moving too quickly.
facts: Mary's aims were threefold: undo religious changes made since 1529 (restoring Papal authority, Catholic practices and monasteries dissolved by Henry); secure a long-term future for Catholicism by marrying and having children; and ensure the Catholic religion was abided by across the country.

Mary's advisors were concerned about the feasibility of some aims. Gardiner was uncertain about restoring papal authority. Imperial ambassador Simon Renard expressed concerns about restoring former monastic property. Even Charles V and Pope Julius III feared Mary would proceed too quickly and provoke unrest that might threaten her position as queen.

Parliament met in October 1553 but refused to repeal the Act of Supremacy, suggesting anti-Papal feeling even among Catholic sympathisers. It did pass a First Act of Repeal which restored the religious situation of 1547. Mary used the royal prerogative to remove the Second Act of Uniformity and restore the Catholic Mass.

In April 1554 there was controversy in Parliament over the issue of ex-monastic land. Landowning MPs refused to reinstate the Heresy Laws until Mary gave assurances regarding their land. In November Mary accepted that ex-monastic land would be left — then the Heresy Laws were revived.

Over the next three years 284 Protestants were burnt at the stake. The Second Act of Repeal (November 1554) repealed all religious legislation approved since 1529 — but protected property rights of those who had bought church land since 1536. In 1556 the 12 Decrees were introduced to improve clerical discipline and remove criticisms people had against Catholicism.

Popular enthusiasm for the restoration: Mary was initially welcomed with bells rung and Parliament opened with a sung mass. However the question is whether this was more to do with her being the legitimate heir rather than her religion.

heading: The Marian burnings
summary: 284 Protestants were burned under Mary's heresy laws, but the burnings were counter-productive and the public reaction was complex and ambiguous.
facts: The heresy laws were revived in 1554 and the burnings continued from February 1555, when John Rogers was the first to be burnt, until Mary's death in 1558.
284 people were burnt at the stake (51 were women). They mostly took place in the south-east, London, Canterbury and Colchester – the Protestant strongholds.

John Foxe's Book of Martyrs highlighted the burnings and coloured our understanding of the impact of the Marian persecutions. He shows there was considerable opposition to the regime. The impact on the public is not clear.

In October 1555, Bishops Ridley and Latimer were burned at Oxford and in March 1556 Cranmer was burned. Before his burning, Cranmer had recanted Protestantism but on the stake he publicly reversed his recantation and denounced the Pope.
Gardiner opposed the burnings, believing them to be counter-productive. However, his death in 1555 meant they continued apace under Pole's direction.
Large numbers attended the burnings. There isn't much evidence of the burnings converting the audience. Many people viewed them as entertainment or a commercial opportunity.

During the early months of 1554 c.800 Protestants began to leave England for Germany and Switzerland. The exiles included many of the printers in England who helped develop an underground Protestant propaganda movement. They kept key Protestant works like Cranmer's Prayer Book and Foxe's Book of Martyrs in circulation.

heading: De facto change under Mary
summary: Despite five years of Catholic restoration, Mary's reign was too short to cement lasting change, though the time it took Elizabeth to re-establish Protestantism suggests the restoration had real impact.
facts: Edward's short reign meant that much of the country, especially the North, had always remained Catholic at a local level. Most church records identify that Catholic worship returned speedily and many welcomed it. The changes would be expensive and lengthy yet people were willing to spend their minimal funds on the Church — chalices, altars and vestments reappeared quickly in many parishes.

At a local level, the Catholic restoration was more successful than the Edwardian Reformation had been. The North and West had always been more resistant to Protestant change; in these regions Mary's restoration was welcomed rather than merely accepted. Even in Protestant strongholds like London and East Anglia, many returned to Catholic practice without visible opposition.

However Mary's reign suffered the same problem as Edward's — five years was insufficient to enact lasting change. Unlike Henry and Edward, Mary faced no popular rebellion on the issue of religion itself — Wyatt's rebellion was primarily about the Spanish marriage. However over 800 clergy were deprived for failing to return to Catholic practices, suggesting a minority of committed Protestants remained.

The Marian exiles presented a particular problem at a local level. They included many of the printers in England who helped develop an underground Protestant propaganda movement, keeping Cranmer's Prayer Book and Foxe's Book of Martyrs in circulation. The government tried to limit Protestant literature but with limited success — the survival of over 19,000 copies of Cranmer's Second Prayer Book demonstrates Protestant networks remained active.

Parliament's opposition was primarily about losing land rather than the religious policies themselves — all other legislation passed without much concern. This suggests the gentry's vested interests in former church land were the main obstacle, not widespread popular opposition to Catholicism.

By not producing an heir Catholicism did not triumph — Elizabeth would not allow it. It is worth noting that the time it took Elizabeth to establish Protestantism (she needed her own Reformation) suggests the Marian regime had been successful in restoring Catholic practice at the local level. The new clergy Elizabeth had to appoint were often reluctant converts who privately remained Catholic.

heading: Socioeconomic causes of unrest
summary: A combination of population rise, debasement, enclosure and Spanish bullion created the Great Price Rise that drove poverty and social tension across the mid-Tudor period.
facts: Inflation had been occurring throughout the 16th century but accelerated in the 1540s. Food prices had doubled since the start of the century. Causes included: population rise (from 2.3 million in 1525 to 3 million in 1551); the end of the Medieval Warm Period and beginning of the Little Ice Age; and Spanish Bullion from the New World inflating European currency.

Debasement: in order to finance wars against France and Scotland in the early 1540s, Henry VIII began a policy of debasement — reducing the amount of precious metal in coinage. Somerset as Protector continued debasement to fund the war against Scotland, worsening inflation. It reduced confidence in the currency and prices rose to compensate.

Enclosure: began to pick up pace in the Tudor period due to the growing cloth market in the Netherlands. English wool was prized and gentry transformed land from agriculture to livestock farming — leading to less food produced, fewer farm hands employed and increased unemployment. Enclosure of common land by the gentry for their own benefit was increasingly controversial.

Commonwealth Men (contemporaries who believed the wealthy had an obligation to the poor) blamed the Great Price Rise on enclosure and greedy gentlemen. They did not understand the impact of the rising population on supply and demand. Somerset commissioned John Hales to investigate enclosures in 1548 — contributing to his reputation as the 'Good Duke'.

The Vagrancy Act of 1547 condemned vagrants to two years' slavery for the first offence — an extreme punishment that proved impossible to enforce and was quickly repealed. There was limited support for the poor since Henry's dissolution of the monasteries had removed a key source of charitable provision.

By 1549 these pressures combined into the 'year of the many-headed monster' — unrest occurred in over half the counties of England, including in Lincolnshire, Somerset, Wiltshire, Hampshire, Kent, Sussex, Essex, Staffordshire, Devon, Cornwall, Yorkshire and beyond. Most were suppressed by local gentry but Kett's and the Western Rebellion needed Royal suppression.

subheadings.label: Population and harvest
facts: Inflation had been occurring throughout the 16th century, but accelerated in the 1540s. Food prices had doubled since the start of the century.

Population rise – Malthusian Crisis: for the first time since the Black Death the population of England was rising. From 1525–1551 the population rose from 2.3 million to 3 million. Agricultural productivity was unable to keep pace and therefore the price of food rose.
Bad harvests were common. This was exacerbated by the end of the Medieval Warm Period and beginning of the Little Ice Age.

subheadings.label: Debasement and enclosure
facts: Debasement: in order to finance wars against France and Scotland in the early 1540s, Henry VIII's government had begun a policy of debasement. Debasement reduced confidence in the currency and so prices rose to compensate. Somerset continued debasement to fund the war against Scotland.

Enclosure began to pick up pace in the Tudor period due to the growing cloth market in the Netherlands. English wool was prized and so many gentry transformed their land from agriculture to livestock farming. This led to less food being produced, higher food prices, and increased unemployment.

Commonwealth men, not understanding the impact of the population rise or debasement, blamed the Great Price Rise on enclosure and greedy gentlemen. This added to the complaints that the gentry and merchant class regularly practiced rack renting and regrating to exploit the poor.

subheadings.label: Impact
facts: Spain's conquest of the New World meant that vast quantities of American gold and silver were being imported into Europe. This meant that across Europe the value of these metals decreased and so the value of coinage decreased, exacerbating price rises.

The Great Price Rise, combined with increasing demand for land, led to high levels of poverty and vagrancy. Fears over increases in vagrancy prompted the Vagrancy Act of 1547 which condemned vagrants to two years slavery for the first offence, and lifetime slavery for a second.

heading: Kett's Rebellion
summary: Kett's Rebellion of 1549 was the most serious of the year's widespread unrest, capturing Norwich before being crushed by Warwick at Dussindale.
facts: The unrest in East Anglia began when a mob attacked the enclosures of John Flowerdew, a local gentleman. Flowerdew redirected the protest to Robert Kett, another gentleman who had also enclosed much land. Somehow Kett became the leader — the rebels soon numbered 16,000. In Norwich in 1549, just 6% of the population owned 60% of the land.

Kett's rebels met in July 1549, marched on Norwich (the second largest city in England) and camped at Mousehold Heath. They then stormed Norwich. Kett ran a well-ordered camp — justice was administered to show they could maintain order. Many of the rebels' demands concerned enclosure and high rents, though there were also complaints about absent or uneducated clergy.

The rebels' demands were politely written to Somerset, demonstrating that the rebels believed central government would support them — their anger was directed primarily at the local gentry, not the government itself.

Government sent over 14,000 troops with Northampton, but they were defeated. Earl Warwick (later Northumberland) came and massacred the rebels at Dussindale — 3,000 were killed. A further 49 of the leaders were executed for treason.

Why it failed: Warwick had 12,000 well-trained and experienced troops from the war with Scotland. Kett was not an experienced military leader — he abandoned his well-defended camp at Mousehold Heath to meet Warwick at Dussindale.

Kett's Rebellion is significant as the most serious of the 1549 rebellions, capturing the important city of Norwich. It contributed directly to Somerset's fall — the Privy Council blamed his enclosure commissions for encouraging the rebels. Warwick's defeat of the rebellion made him indispensable and paved the way for his rise to power.

heading: The Western Rebellion
summary: The Western or Prayer Book Rebellion of 1549 was primarily a religious reaction to the First Book of Common Prayer, though economic grievances also played a role.
facts: A prelude to the unrest was the brutal murder of William Body in 1548. Body had been tasked by the government to supervise iconoclasm in Cornwall — which was extremely unpopular. The murder demonstrated the depth of resistance to religious change in the region.

There was large opposition to the First Book of Common Prayer enforced in early 1549. Many wanted the return of the old Latin services — partly because they did not follow the new religion and partly because many Cornishmen were more familiar with Latin than English. The list of demands produced by the rebels was almost entirely religious.

However there is evidence that early demands excluded by the clergy included demands about high taxes and rents — supported by the actions of the rebels chanting 'Kill all the Gentlemen' at Bodmin. This suggests enclosure and inflation caused the unrest alongside religion.

The rebels initially gathered at Sampford Courtenay and then marched on Exeter, besieging the city for around a month. After around a month, a government force of 8,000 led by Lord John Russell defeated the rebels at Sampford Courtenay. Over 3,000 were executed.

Why it failed: unlike the unrest in East Anglia, the Western Rebellion had no clear leadership. Different sections of the rebels attacked different targets. There was limited military leadership — they were no match for experienced government forces.

Significance: the scale of executions — over 3,000 — demonstrates the government's fear of the scale of the rebellion. 1549 was 'the year of the many-headed monster' — the most widespread unrest of the Tudor period, requiring soldiers to be diverted from the Scottish border, weakening Somerset's foreign policy.

heading: Wyatt's Rebellion: causes
summary: Wyatt's Rebellion of 1554 was ostensibly caused by opposition to the Spanish marriage, though religion, factional grievances and economic decline all played a role.
facts: The rebellion began in Kent — a more Protestant area with trading links to Protestant Northern Europe. The timing, immediately after Mary proposed the marriage to Philip in Parliament in November 1553, supports the view that opposition to the Spanish marriage was the main cause.

Many leaders of the rebellion, including Wyatt, had lost positions at court due to their faith — this may have been an attempt to regain their old power. The government's chronicler John Proctor blamed religion as the main cause, though he would be unlikely to accept popular opposition to Philip.

The collapse of the cloth trade in the 1550s particularly affected Kent, creating unemployment and economic grievances. The rebels' chant 'We are all Englishmen' suggests xenophobic opposition to Spanish influence rather than straightforwardly religious motivation.
Wyatt's rebellion planned to replace Mary with Elizabeth, who was to be married to Edward Courtenay, Earl of Devon. However Courtenay disclosed the plot to Stephen Gardiner.
Having been discovered, the rebels had to act immediately. Only Wyatt in Kent did — the other planned risings failed to materialise. Wyatt raised 3,000 men and began to march on London.

A government force led by the Duke of Norfolk was sent to face the rebels — but the government soldiers deserted Norfolk and joined Wyatt's men declaring 'We are all Englishmen'. Mary stood resolutely, made her famous speech at Guildhall which secured the support of Londoners who refused to open the city gates to Wyatt. The royal forces defeated Wyatt's rebellion.

subheadings.label: The Spanish marriage
facts: Mary's marriage to Philip of Spain led to concerns over a foreign marriage and that patronage would be given to the Spanish and that England would be dragged into the Habsburg's wars.
The timing of the rebellion, immediately after Mary proposed the marriage in parliament, would support this. Wyatt had previously been loyal to Mary during the Lady Jane Grey affair.

facts: However xenophobia may have been a useful tool to rally mass support, hiding other causes.

Religion: the rebellion began in Kent, a more Protestant area with trading links to Protestant Northern Europe. Many of the leaders were Protestant including Thomas Wyatt. Part of the plot was to replace Mary with Elizabeth who would defend Protestantism.

subheadings.label: Economic causes
facts: The government's chronicler John Proctor blamed religion as the main cause. However he would be unlikely to accept popular opposition to Philip.
Many leaders of the rebellion, including Wyatt, had lost positions at court due to their faith. This was an attempt to regain their old power.
Collapse of the cloth trade in the 1550s particularly affected Kent creating some unemployment.

heading: Wyatt's Rebellion: consequences
summary: Wyatt's Rebellion failed due to the premature rising and Mary's decisive leadership, but its consequences shaped the rest of her reign.
facts: Wyatt and the leaders were executed. Lady Jane Grey and Guildford Dudley — who had taken no part in the rebellion — were also executed as Mary feared they would become a future Protestant rallying point. Elizabeth was imprisoned in the Tower, though there was no evidence directly connecting her to the plot.

Mary's strength and leadership in making the Guildhall speech — against her Council's advice to leave London — was crucial. It demonstrated that female monarchs could exercise decisive leadership and rally their subjects.

The rebellion's failure confirmed Mary's determination to proceed with the Spanish marriage and the Catholic restoration. It showed there were limits to popular opposition to both — neither the xenophobia about Philip nor Protestant opposition to Catholicism was strong enough to overthrow a determined monarch with London's support.

However the rebellion revealed that Protestantism was not easily eradicated — it had a significant foothold in Kent and other Protestant areas. Elizabeth's imprisonment created a period of danger that might have ended the Protestant cause entirely.

The Privy Council was streamlined following the rebellion — 'casual councillors' were excluded from key committees in 1554. In 1555 Mary established an 'inner council' so only her most valued advisors were present. The rebellion contributed to an improvement in the efficiency of Mary's government.

The rebellion also demonstrated the limits of conspiracy — without widespread popular or noble support, it was relatively easily crushed. This was a lesson that would apply to later plots against Elizabeth: only plots with significant backing — ideally foreign military support — had any realistic chance of success.

facts: Wyatt and the leaders were executed, and Elizabeth was imprisoned in the Tower.

Reasons for failure: the discovery of the plot meant the rebels were forced to rise in Winter. This meant fewer peasants were willing to join. Only one of the four forces rebelled as the other leaders got cold feet. Mary's strength and leadership ensured the rebellion was ultimately defeated.

Consequences: Lady Jane Grey and Guildford Dudley were executed. Elizabeth was imprisoned in the Tower, though released after Wyatt refused to implicate her under torture. Mary proceeded with the marriage to Philip.

heading: Religious pressures in 1558
summary: Elizabeth faced a complex set of domestic and international religious pressures in 1558 that shaped the nature of her Religious Settlement.
facts: England and Europe had been consumed by religious conflict between the Protestant Reformation and Catholic Counter-Reformation for 25 years before Elizabeth's accession. Elizabeth's priority was to 'settle' the matter of religion — but what form this settlement would take was determined by a number of pressures.

The Marian Exiles: approximately 800 leading Protestants had fled England at the start of Mary's reign, basing themselves in the Protestant hotspots of Zurich, Frankfurt and Geneva where many had become more radical, educated with the teachings of John Calvin or Huldrych Zwingli. Calvinism and Zwinglism were threats to Elizabeth as they denied the need for an episcopacy — the church hierarchy which the monarch was said to have no role in.

English Catholics: under Mary's reign Catholicism had been restored by law. Much of the population — particularly in regions furthest from the centre of power like the North — had never left Catholicism. Due to the Pope's refusal to grant Henry VIII's divorce, many Catholics viewed Elizabeth as illegitimate and believed Mary, Queen of Scots was the true Queen of England.

The powerful Catholic bishops inherited from Mary all held seats in the House of Lords and could block legislative changes. Fortunately for Elizabeth, the Archbishop of Canterbury Reginald Pole had died the same day as Mary, so she could appoint her own Protestant Archbishop (Matthew Parker). Approximately 1/3 of the powerful English nobility and gentry retained the Catholic faith privately.

The international situation: Elizabeth inherited from Mary a war with France and an alliance with Spain through Mary's marriage to Philip. Spain and France were the two richest and most powerful countries in the world — both strongly Catholic. Elizabeth's political future depended on the Habsburg-Valois rivalry between them continuing.

Scotland was a complication. Mary Queen of Scots was a Catholic monarch married to the French Dauphin. Scotland was ruled by Mary's French Catholic mother, Mary of Guise. King Henry II of France presented Mary as the true queen of England. In 1559 Scottish Protestant Lords overthrew Mary of Guise and made Scotland Protestant in Mary's absence.

facts: c.800 leading Protestants had fled England at the start of Mary I's reign. In their exile they had based themselves in the Protestant hotspots of Zurich, Frankfurt and Geneva where many had become more radical, educated with the teachings of John Calvin or Huldrych Zwingli.

Under Mary I's reign Catholicism had been restored to England by law. Even without this restoration, much of the English population had never left Catholicism. The powerful bishops Elizabeth inherited from Mary were all Catholics.

Due to the Pope's refusal to grant Henry VIII's divorce from Catherine of Aragon, many Catholics viewed Elizabeth as illegitimate and thus not the true Queen. Instead they believed Mary, Queen of Scots was the true Queen of England.

Scotland was a complication. Mary, Queen of Scots was a Catholic monarch but had been living in France since 1548 and was married to the French Dauphin, Francis. King Henry II of France presented Mary as the true queen of England.
Elizabeth was the child of Henry VIII and Anne Boleyn. She symbolised a Protestant England and was raised Protestant. However she did not share the religious zeal of either of her half-siblings.

heading: The Religious Settlement
summary: The Religious Settlement of 1559 established a deliberately ambiguous via media, designed to accommodate as many subjects as possible.
facts: Act of Supremacy: removed the Pope's authority over the English Church. Made Elizabeth Supreme Governor of the Church (not Supreme Head, to avoid alienating Catholics who believed only a man could be head of the Church). Elizabeth was in charge of a strict episcopal hierarchy of Archbishops and Bishops. Mary's heresy laws were repealed — no more burnings.

Act of Uniformity: Cranmer's 1552 Book of Common Prayer was used in all churches. However the most radical passage — the 'Black Rubric' that explicitly denied Transubstantiation — was omitted. During Holy Communion, wording from both the 1552 and the more conservative 1548 Prayer Books was used, allowing open interpretation of Transubstantiation or Consubstantiation.

Everyone must attend a licensed Church of England service on a Sunday. Those failing to do so would be guilty of recusancy and charged 1 shilling — the average weekly wage of a labourer, and a manageable punishment for the gentry and nobility.

The Royal Injunctions: church taxes (First Fruits and Tenths) to be paid to the Crown; the few small monasteries Mary had restored were dissolved again; clergy were to wear distinctive vestments; music was encouraged and images accepted; clergy could marry. These represented a compromise between the 1547 and 1553 positions.

Via Media: Elizabeth described the Settlement as Via Media — 'the middle way'. It was designed to be an acceptable compromise for Catholics and radical Protestants that would cease religious conflict. In practice many were dissatisfied — but the Settlement endured throughout Elizabeth's reign.

Enforcement was patchy, especially in the North where many clergy quietly continued Catholic practices. The Court of High Commission (the highest ecclesiastical court), visitations by bishops and the Privy Council all enforced the Settlement — but without sufficient trained Protestant clergy, enforcement had real limits.

heading: Getting the Settlement through Parliament
summary: The Settlement faced serious opposition in the House of Lords from Catholic bishops, requiring Elizabeth to use prorogation and compromise to get it passed.
facts: Elizabeth could not use proclamations or decrees to enact religious change — she needed to get the Settlement through Parliament to give it legitimacy and make it enforceable. This was not anticipated to be a problem as neither Edward nor Mary had encountered significant parliamentary opposition to their religious changes.

However in the 1559 Parliament the Catholic bishops and some Catholic lay nobles in the House of Lords showed they would oppose and alter the Settlement — in particular making Elizabeth 'Head of the Church' rather than the more moderate 'Supreme Governor'.

Elizabeth responded by proroguing Parliament over the Easter of 1559 to delay. She arrested two of the more vocal critics — the Bishops of Lincoln and Winchester — for disobedience. She compromised by adopting the title 'Supreme Governor' instead of 'Supreme Head'.

The Settlement passed the House of Lords by a margin of just three votes — suggesting the Catholic opposition in the Lords was much stronger than anticipated. Elizabeth was then able to remove the Marian bishops when they refused to swear the Oath of Loyalty.

The difficulty in passing the Settlement revealed the depth of Catholic sentiment in the Lords. Elizabeth's management of the crisis — through prorogation, compromise on the title and removal of recalcitrant bishops — demonstrated her political skill in achieving her aims while maintaining the appearance of consensus.

heading: The Puritan challenge: Parliament
summary: Puritan MPs attempted to push Elizabeth towards a more radical Protestant settlement through parliament, but Elizabeth consistently defended her royal prerogative over religious matters.
facts: The historian John Neale argued that a small but highly organised group of Puritan MPs — the 'Puritan Choir' — attempted to alter the Religious Settlement through Acts of Parliament. Other historians have criticised Neale's interpretation and suggested that Puritan influence in parliament only increased in the 1600s. In the 1559 Parliament only 19 Marian exiles were MPs.

Strickland's Proposals (1571): Puritan MP Walter Strickland attempted to alter the Book of Common Prayer to remove vestments, the ring in marriage and kneeling at communion — all deemed Catholic superstitions. Strickland was summoned before the Privy Council for infringing the Royal Prerogative and barred from Parliament. Whilst he was allowed to return, his bill was never heard of again.

Cope's Proposals (1586): Anthony Cope MP made an extremely radical 'bill and book' proposal that would replace the Book of Common Prayer with the more radical Genevan Prayer Book and remove the episcopacy within the Church. Several Puritan MPs vocally supported the proposals. Cope and four supporters were sent to the Tower of London. The bill was defeated.

The Puritan Peter Wentworth MP continued complaints in the Parliaments of 1571, 1576, 1587 and 1593. He argued Parliament's right to discuss religion and the succession. In 1576 he compared Elizabeth's involvement in Parliament to the work of the devil. The majority of Parliament did not support the Wentworths — in 1576 the House of Commons interrupted Peter Wentworth's speech and sent him to the Tower themselves without Elizabeth's involvement.

Elizabeth consistently framed religious matters as part of the Royal Prerogative — beyond parliamentary competence. Puritan MPs were never able to force lasting change through Parliament, and Elizabeth's management of the Speaker and ability to prorogue meant she retained control.

heading: The Puritan challenge: clergy and separatism
summary: Puritans challenged the settlement from within the Church through the Vestiarian Controversy, popular pamphlets, and ultimately separatist movements.
facts: The Vestiarian Controversy: Puritans despised the wearing of vestments as they signified clergy to be holy men separate to ordinary worshippers. Many refused to wear the vestments. The Archbishop of Canterbury Matthew Parker compromised in his 1566 Advertisements — he conceded that clergy could wear simply 'a comely surplice with long sleeves' at Communion and did not have to wear vestments for the remainder of the service. However 37 Puritan clergymen who refused to accept Parker's compromise lost their jobs. Henry Bullinger (Zwingli's successor) advised the Puritans to back down over such minor issues.

The 39 Articles were the central ordinances of the new Church of England, initially agreed by the Convocation in 1563. However many were resisted by Puritans as they were not seen as radical enough. In 1571 it was conceded that clergy with reservations need not follow the ceremonial articles. However all clergy had to follow doctrinal articles — this was non-negotiable.

Cartwright's Criticisms: Cambridge Presbyterian professor Thomas Cartwright gave a series of lectures in 1570 strongly denouncing the hierarchy in the Church. He lost his professorship and his freedom of speech. Admonition to Parliament (1572): John Field and Thomas Wilcox penned a public criticism of Parliament calling for the end of Church episcopacy. Field and Wilcox were imprisoned for a year but the admonition did circulate amongst the literate population.

Marprelate Tracts (1588-89): a series of Puritan pamphlets issued under the pseudonym Martin Marprelate. They alienated many moderates with their vicious and provocative attacks on bishops. They allowed the Privy Council to suppress the printing presses producing the tracts.

Separatist challenge: several Puritan groups attempted to establish an independent Puritan Church. A lack of central organisation and agreement of beliefs and methods doomed this movement. 1581 Brownist Church led by Robert Browne in Norwich — after spells in prison they fled to the Netherlands. 1590s a new Separatist movement was led by Henry Barrow and John Greenwood in London — the leaders were arrested and executed in 1593.

Survival of Puritanism: survived through prophesyings and the classis movement as well as the protection of Privy Councillors like Leicester. However internal divisions, incoherent methods and suppression led by Whitgift hugely limited the movement.

heading: Elizabeth's archbishops
summary: Elizabeth's three archbishops of Canterbury each shaped the Church's response to Puritanism in different ways, from Parker's compromise to Whitgift's repression.
facts: Matthew Parker (1559-75): Parker had previously been Anne Boleyn's chaplain. He was a Protestant but had not gone into exile during the reign of Mary and was thus not radicalised by the ideas of Calvin and Zwingli. For Elizabeth, he was the perfect man to enact her Via Media. Parker defended the Religious Settlement by overseeing the passage of the 39 Articles at the Convocation of 1563 — resisting Puritan attempts to introduce more radical doctrinal and ceremonial changes. These changes were defeated by a single vote. He reached a compromise with the Puritans during the Vestiarian Controversy in his 1566 Advertisements.

Edmund Grindal (1575-83): unlike Parker, Grindal was a former Marian exile and had been a key contributor to Foxe's Book of Martyrs. When Elizabeth purged Mary's Catholic bishops after the 1559 Parliament, she had limited candidates for new Protestant bishops and was forced to accept some more radical than her liking. Grindal was one of these and was sympathetic to Puritan concerns. In the 1570s Grindal came into conflict with Elizabeth over prophesyings. Elizabeth was concerned these were being used to instil new clergy with Puritan ideas and ferment rebellion. Elizabeth ordered Grindal to suppress these prophesyings in 1576 but he refused. Grindal was suspended in 1577 and confined to house arrest until his death in 1583.

John Whitgift (1583-1604): after her conflict with Grindal, Elizabeth needed a loyal clergyman who would maintain her settlement and stamp out the Puritans. Like Parker, Whitgift had stayed in England during Mary's reign. Whitgift had previously pleased Elizabeth as Vice-Chancellor of Cambridge in the early 1570s — it was he who had ensured Cartwright had lost his professorship. As Archbishop Whitgift sought to take action against non-conformists: he sought to stamp out the Puritan Classis movement of the 1580s; swiftly suppressed those responsible for the Marprelate Tracts in 1588-9; used the Court of High Commission to root out non-conformists; used the Three Articles as a test to find Puritans.

Around 300 Puritan clergy were successfully removed by Whitgift's methods. Cecil initially criticised the Three Articles as too inquisitorial. Elizabeth supported Whitgift strongly and died holding his hand in 1603.

facts: John Whitgift (1583–1604): after her conflict with Grindal, Elizabeth needed a loyal Archbishop. Whitgift used the Court of High Commission to root out non-conformists and issued the Three Articles as a test — clergy had to swear that Elizabeth had sovereignty over all Church matters, that the Book of Common Prayer was the only one to be used, and that the 39 Articles were agreeable to God.

Around 300 Puritan clergy were removed by Whitgift's methods. Cecil initially criticised the Three Articles as 'too inquisitorial'. But Whitgift showed that determined repression could contain though not eliminate the Puritan challenge.

Elizabeth supported Whitgift strongly throughout his archiepiscopacy — she died holding his hand in 1603. The contrast between Grindal's defiance and Whitgift's loyalty illustrates Elizabeth's insistence on control of the Church as part of her Royal Prerogative.

heading: The Catholic threat before 1568
summary: The Catholic threat in the first decade of Elizabeth's reign was limited, largely because of Elizabeth's relative tolerance and the Habsburg-Valois rivalry that prevented coordinated Catholic action.
facts: For the first decade of Elizabeth's reign there was limited overt Catholic challenge. This was largely due to Elizabeth's relative tolerance. The heresy laws were repealed in the Religious Settlement and the sole punishment was a recusancy fine of 1 shilling. For the Catholic gentry and nobility this was a manageable punishment.

Many Church Papists attended Elizabeth's Church of England services before later attending secret Catholic services. Elizabeth and her councillors were aware of this but tolerated it. Elizabeth promised that she 'would not open windows unto men's souls' — she only demanded outward conformity. She did not persecute and even allowed northern JPs to avoid implementing recusancy fines.

Elizabeth's refusal to create martyrs meant that for the majority of Catholics there was no need to overtly oppose the Settlement. They could continue their faith in secret. The absence of trained Catholic priests meant that Catholicism was dying out naturally without the need for persecution.

The Pope's 1570 excommunication was in many ways too little, too late. It came after the English had had 11 years to get used to the Settlement and after the Northern Rising had been crushed. The Habsburg-Valois rivalry between Spain and France prevented the great Catholic powers working together to eradicate Protestantism. Philip of Spain was terrified by the prospect of his greatest rival France having control over England if Mary Queen of Scots came to the throne.

During the 1560s both Spain and France became embroiled in costly internal religious conflicts: 1566-1648 Spain was attempting to suppress the Protestant Dutch Revolt; 1562-98 the French Wars of Religion raged between the Catholic League and the Huguenots. England became less of a priority.

heading: Mary Queen of Scots
summary: The arrival of Mary Queen of Scots in England in 1568 transformed the Catholic threat — giving it a credible alternative monarch around which plots could form.
facts: When Mary returned to Scotland in 1561 she found a country ruled by the Protestant Lords. Mary tried to rule as a Catholic monarch but was forced to abdicate in 1567 following her suspected involvement in the assassination of her second husband Lord Darnley. In 1568 Mary fled to northern England seeking Elizabeth's support.

Mary was a real danger to Elizabeth as she was Elizabeth's cousin and next in line to the throne. If Mary succeeded as Queen she would likely restore Catholicism to England. More concerningly, many of Elizabeth's Catholic subjects already viewed Mary as the true Queen of England.

Mary's arrival in the highly Catholic North of England in 1568 provided a figurehead around which Catholic plots would ferment. Even under house arrest, where Elizabeth placed her, Mary acted as a 'lightning rod' for Catholic opposition.

Elizabeth placed Mary under house arrest — Mary was too dangerous to release (a Catholic claimant to the English throne) but too politically sensitive to execute or return to Scotland. This solution satisfied nobody and left the problem unresolved for nearly 20 years.

Mary's presence meant that every Catholic plot from 1568 onwards had a potential Catholic successor ready to take the throne. This made the plots far more dangerous than anything Elizabeth had faced in the first decade of her reign.

heading: The Rising of the North
summary: The Rising of the North (1569) was the most serious domestic rebellion of Elizabeth's reign — a Catholic uprising in support of Mary Queen of Scots that was crushed without significant noble support.
facts: A plot to marry Mary to the powerful Duke of Norfolk to strengthen her claim to the English throne was uncovered. In desperation, the Catholic northern Earls of Northumberland and Westmoreland launched an uprising. The rebels captured Durham and held Catholic Latin mass in the Cathedral. A summons was issued to other Catholic nobility and gentry. None answered the call.

A royal army led by the Earl of Sussex marched north and the rebels fled without fighting a major battle. Mary was moved to Coventry, away from the Catholic North. Elizabeth resisted calls from her Privy Council to execute the Duke of Norfolk. However she did execute 450 rebels.

In 1570 Pope Pius V issued his Papal bull Regnans in Excelsis which excommunicated Elizabeth. Catholics were now absolved of any loyalty to Elizabeth. This transformed the Catholic threat from passive non-conformity to active potential treachery and dramatically escalated the government's legislative response.

The Rising was the largest armed challenge to Elizabeth's authority and showed the danger that Mary's presence posed as a Catholic figurehead. However the failure of other Catholic nobles to answer the summons showed how limited active Catholic opposition actually was.

heading: The Catholic plots
summary: A series of Catholic plots against Elizabeth culminated in the Babington Plot, which provided the evidence needed to execute Mary Queen of Scots.
facts: In 1584 Philip II and the French Catholic League led by the Duke of Guise signed the Treaty of Joinville — a Catholic alliance primarily to prevent the Protestant Henry of Navarre becoming King of France, but with the potential for joint Catholic action against Elizabeth.

Discovered by William Cecil. Norfolk was executed in 1572 but Elizabeth resisted calls to execute Mary.

heading: Seminary priests and Jesuits
summary: The arrival of seminary priests from Douai and Jesuits from Rome from the 1570s revitalised English Catholicism and dramatically escalated the government's response.
facts: Elizabeth's hope that the lack of trained Catholic priests would lead to Catholicism dying out was countered by the efforts of William Allen, an exiled Catholic Cardinal from his Seminary 'The English College' at Douai in France.

The first Seminary Priests trained by Allen arrived in 1574. By 1585, 279 Seminary Priests had travelled to England. The Jesuits were another order of Catholic priests who also came to England in the 1580s to restore Catholicism. In total around 650 Jesuits or Seminary Priests were active in England. Many were sheltered by Catholic nobility and gentry in priest holes.

Government response: 1571 — it was made treason to possess or distribute a copy of the Papal Bull of excommunication. 1581 — recusancy fines increased to £20 a month and converting someone to Catholicism became treason. 1585 — all Catholic priests expelled from England. Any priest remaining in England, or anyone found harbouring a priest, was to be executed. 133 Seminary Priests and Jesuits were executed as a result.

heading: Problems facing the Catholics
summary: Despite the plots and priests, English Catholics faced overwhelming obstacles that limited the threat they posed to Elizabeth's settlement.
facts: In the period 1558-1589 the Catholic threat was constrained by several factors. Elizabeth's tolerance: the Religious Settlement's punishment for recusancy was just 1 shilling — a manageable sum for the gentry and nobility. Elizabeth promised outward conformity, liberty of conscience — many Catholics attended Church of England services and secret Catholic services (Church Papists). Elizabeth's refusal to create martyrs removed a key rallying point.

Elizabeth's tolerance was genuine in the early period. She did not persecute and even allowed northern JPs to avoid implementing recusancy fines. For the first decade of her reign there was limited overt Catholic challenge — the heresy laws were repealed and Catholicism was dying out naturally without trained priests to sustain it.

The Habsburg-Valois rivalry between Spain and France prevented joint Catholic action against England throughout the 1560s. Spain was fighting the expensive Dutch Revolt (1566-1648); France was consumed by the Wars of Religion (1562-98). Philip of Spain actually persuaded Pope Pius IV not to excommunicate Elizabeth in 1563 — fearing French dominance of England more than he feared Protestant England.

The excommunication of 1570 came too little too late — it came after the English had had eleven years to get used to the Settlement and after the Northern Rising had already been crushed. The arrival of seminary priests from 1574 and Jesuits from 1580 changed the nature of the Catholic threat — from passive survival to active mission — and forced the government to escalate its response with the legislation of 1581 and 1585.

Elizabeth's longevity was the ultimate obstacle for English Catholics in this period. Both Edward VI (six years) and Mary I (five years) were unable to cement their religious changes. Elizabeth was on the throne for 45 years. During her long reign the Catholic establishment from Mary's reign died out. The new generation of gentry, nobility and clergy all grew up under Elizabeth's Settlement.

After Mary Queen of Scots's execution in 1587 Catholic plots became far less dangerous as they had lost their potential monarch. No Catholic candidate for the throne had anywhere near the legitimacy or support that Mary had commanded. The defeat of the Spanish Armada in 1588 ended the most serious external Catholic threat. By 1589 the Catholic cause in England was effectively defeated.

heading: Overview of national government
summary: Elizabethan government operated through a triangle of monarch, Privy Council and Parliament, with the monarch retaining supreme authority through the royal prerogative.
facts: Role of the Monarch: the monarch was believed to derive their power directly from God. All legislation had to be approved by the monarch's Royal Assent. Unlike today the monarch had every right to veto legislation they did not approve of. The monarch was responsible for managing law and order and the defence of the realm, expected to manage the finances, could issue Royal Proclamations that were expected to be followed, and had the power to call, prorogue and dissolve Parliament at will.

The Royal Prerogative were the issues that only the monarch had the right to decide — they included: religion, the succession and foreign policy. The monarch presided at Court where they were surrounded by their courtiers.

Role of the Privy Council: the council of the monarch's most important advisors, with a maximum of 20 members. It met several times a week and daily during the 1590s. Key figures including the Secretary of State and Lord Treasurer. Most councillors were also courtiers and prominent MPs. The Privy Council managed Parliament by setting the parliamentary agenda, influencing the election of Speaker and promoting their supporters to be MPs. Dominated for most of the reign by William Cecil.

Role of Parliament: could pass legislation which was more permanent and enforceable than a proclamation. The monarch needed the approval of Parliament to gain taxation — Parliament could withhold grants of taxation until their grievances were addressed. Called ten times during Elizabeth's reign (over thirteen sessions).

The House of Commons: MPs tended to be members of the gentry, elected or nominated by a very small group of knights and merchants. The House of Lords included the Lords Temporal (the earls and dukes of England) and Lords Spiritual (the 26 bishops of the Church of England). Legislation had to be approved by both Houses before being sent for Royal Assent.

heading: The role of gender
summary: Elizabeth's gender shaped every aspect of her reign — how she governed, how she presented herself, and how her councillors, Parliament and foreign powers related to her.
facts: Elizabeth was only the second woman to rule England in her own right. Mary I's reign had been associated in Protestant memory with burning and a disastrous Spanish marriage. Elizabeth inherited deeply ingrained assumptions that women could not lead armies, control powerful men, or exercise the authority that monarchy required. John Knox's First Blast of the Trumpet Against the Monstrous Regiment of Women (1558) articulated the most extreme version of this view.

Elizabeth's response was to construct a carefully managed public image that transcended gender. She adopted the language of monarchy regardless of sex — at Tilbury she declared 'I have the body of a weak, feeble woman; but I have the heart and stomach of a king, and of a king of England too.' She presented herself simultaneously as the Virgin Queen (devoted to England, needing no husband) and as Gloriana (powerful, divinely favoured, invincible).

Gender shaped the succession question more than any other issue. Parliament and the Privy Council repeatedly urged Elizabeth to marry and produce an heir — not simply because they wanted an heir but because they assumed a queen needed a king to govern effectively. Elizabeth's refusal to name a successor was framed as a uniquely female failing — a reluctance to face hard political realities.

Gender affected Elizabeth's management of faction. She used her femininity deliberately — courtiers competed for her personal affection, making loyalty to the Queen partly an emotional rather than purely political relationship. This gave Elizabeth a tool that male monarchs did not have. Leicester, Essex, Hatton and Raleigh all sought to be her favourite as much as her minister.

Gender shaped the Religious Settlement. Elizabeth could not be called Supreme Head of the Church — the title was theologically objectionable for a woman — and so the compromise title Supreme Governor was adopted. This actually made the Settlement more acceptable to Catholics who could not accept a woman as head of the Church.

Foreign policy was deeply affected by gender. Potential marriage alliances dominated diplomacy for the first twenty years of Elizabeth's reign. Philip II of Spain initially supported Elizabeth partly because he feared the alternative — Mary Queen of Scots and French dominance. The question of who Elizabeth would marry was a central tool of foreign policy throughout the 1560s and 1570s.

heading: Key figures on the Privy Council
summary: Elizabeth's most important councillors dominated government throughout her reign, with Cecil providing administrative stability and Walsingham intelligence and security.
facts: William Cecil (Lord Burghley from 1571): Cecil was Elizabeth's principal advisor until his death in 1598. He held the posts of Secretary of State until 1572, then Lord Treasurer from 1572 to his death. He was an extremely hard-working and loyal advisor. He helped draft the Religious Settlement, managed Elizabeth's correspondence, created an intelligence service to discover plots and ran the Privy Council. Cecil was by nature a cautious and pragmatic man.

Robert Dudley (Earl of Leicester from 1564): Dudley was a close friend of Elizabeth, perhaps since they had both been imprisoned in the Tower during the reign of Mary I. Dudley was promoted more for his personality than his political skill — he was tall, handsome, charismatic and witty. Dudley's wife Amy Robsart had died in mysterious circumstances in 1560, which was the subject of much rumour. Despite his flash personality, Dudley was a Puritan and often championed military intervention to protect Protestants in France and the Netherlands.

Sir Francis Walsingham: a protege of Cecil with a similar loyalty to Elizabeth and sober work-ethic. Took over running of the intelligence service and role of Secretary of State in 1573. Also a devout Puritan who hated Mary, Queen of Scots.

Thomas Howard, Duke of Norfolk: the most senior nobleman in England and the only Duke. Raised Protestant but with strong Catholic familial links. Executed in 1572 for his role in the Rising of the North and Ridolfi Plot.

Robert Devereux, Earl of Essex: rose to Elizabeth's court as the godson of Leicester and due to his marriage to the daughter of Francis Walsingham. Essex's wit, eloquence and dashing personality quickly made him a favourite of the ageing Elizabeth in the 1590s. Raised to the Privy Council in 1593. Essex frequently acted unilaterally — joining Drake's English Armada in 1589 against Elizabeth's direct orders; disobeying orders to confer with Henry IV of France in 1592 without Elizabeth's permission. Executed for treason in 1601.

Sir Robert Cecil: son of William Cecil. Rose to Secretary of State in 1596 whilst Essex was at Cadiz. From 1601 onwards dominated government unopposed. Managed the smooth transition of power to James I in 1603.

heading: Elizabeth's management of faction
summary: Elizabeth deliberately encouraged factional competition among her councillors, using personal charm and calculated delay to prevent any single minister from dominating.
facts: Elizabeth stayed aloof of faction, and in fact encouraged such disputes to get a wider debate on certain issues. By taking her time before making decisions, Elizabeth did not show favour to any particular faction and was not easily swayed by her Councillors. Elizabeth used her gender to manage loyalty as courtiers and Councillors would compete for her affection.

A key recurring cause of contention in the Council was Elizabeth's potential suitors: 1565-66 Leicester came into dispute with a faction led by Norfolk and his cousin the Earl of Sussex. Norfolk accused Leicester of having murdered Amy Robsart in order to marry Elizabeth. The factions wore identifying ribbons at court. Elizabeth ended the dispute by making it clear she would not marry Leicester. 1567, Cecil promoted Archduke Charles of Austria as a potential suitor — Leicester used anti-Catholic propaganda against Charles to scupper the marriage.
Similarly in 1579-84 Leicester used anti-Catholic propaganda to whip up public opposition to Burghley's proposed suitor the French Duke of Alencon.

1578-85, The Dutch Revolt divided the Council. Leicester and Walsingham, as devout Puritans, urged direct intervention to support the Dutch rebels. The more watchful Burghley urged caution for fear of risking Spanish retaliation and an expensive and threatening war. Elizabeth refrained from siding either way until the assassination of the rebel leader William of Orange in 1585 forced her intervention.

Mary, Queen of Scots was an issue that united the Council against Elizabeth. Repeatedly the Council petitioned Elizabeth to execute Mary. They agreed the Bond of Association in 1584 to force the matter. In 1562, during Elizabeth's near-fatal illness with Smallpox, she asked the Privy Council to make Robert Dudley Protector of the Realm. There was much relief from Cecil when Elizabeth recovered.
