heading: Managing Parliament
summary: Elizabeth used a range of tools to manage Parliament, from prorogation and the royal veto to controlling the Speaker and exploiting the Privy Council's influence.
facts: If Elizabeth disapproved of a particular batch of MPs she could dissolve Parliament — then when she called a new Parliament, new MPs would be elected. Alternatively Elizabeth could prorogue Parliament which would suspend it for as long as she liked. During the suspension she or her Privy Council could put pressure on MPs to change their position.

The Privy Council were expected to promote Elizabeth's wishes in Parliament. Many Councillors were prominent politicians who dominated Parliamentary business. Elizabeth and the Privy Council influenced the choice of Speaker of the House of Commons who controlled debates, chose who could speak and thus controlled the Commons.

If a bill that Elizabeth disapproved of managed to pass both Houses of Parliament, Elizabeth could use her Royal Veto to reject the proposed law. As a last resort, Elizabeth had the ability to arrest MPs who directly challenged her prerogative as traitors. However such an aggressive use of royal power could potentially increase parliamentary opposition.

The traditional interpretation of John Neale argued that Elizabeth's relationship with Parliament was one of conflict. He saw Parliament as a radical body dominated by Puritan gentry who pushed for religious reform and greater parliamentary privileges. Revisionist historians including Geoffrey Elton argued that any conflict was rarely prolonged and that Elizabeth's relationship with Parliament was mainly one of co-operation as they shared similar aims for the stability of England and the protection of the Protestant settlement.

heading: Conflict in Parliament

facts: Over religion: Puritan MPs repeatedly attempted to alter the Religious Settlement through Parliament. 1571 Parliament — Strickland's Bill. Strickland was questioned by the Privy Council for infringing on the Royal Prerogative before being suspended from Parliament. This caused some outcry and so Strickland was allowed to return but his bill was never seen again. 1586 Parliament — Cope's Proposals. Cope and four supporters were sent to the Tower of London and the Privy Council, led by Christopher Hatton, argued against the bill. It was defeated.

Over marriage and the succession: many MPs were concerned that if Elizabeth remained unmarried and had no heir then after Elizabeth's death the throne would fall to the Catholic Mary, Queen of Scots. In the 1559 and 1563 Parliaments Elizabeth was presented with petitions that she should marry. In the 1566 Parliament the issue was seen as extremely important following Elizabeth's near-fatal experience of Smallpox in 1562. William Cecil himself helped organise the delegation from Parliament requesting she name a successor. Elizabeth reduced her subsidy request by 1/3 to appease Parliament.

Over freedom of speech: Elizabeth's rigid defence of the Royal Prerogative angered some MPs who believed Parliament should have the freedom to discuss these issues. 1566 — Paul Wentworth MP criticised Elizabeth's denial of Parliament's rights. The Puritan Peter Wentworth MP continued these complaints in the Parliaments of 1571, 1576, 1587 and 1593. In 1576 he compared Elizabeth's involvement in Parliament to the work of the devil. The majority of Parliament did not support the Wentworths — in 1576 the House of Commons itself interrupted Peter Wentworth's speech and sent him to the Tower without Elizabeth's involvement.

heading: Marriage and the succession
summary: Elizabeth's refusal to marry or name a successor was a calculated political strategy, though it created serious constitutional uncertainty and fuelled factional conflict.
facts: It was expected that Elizabeth would marry and produce an heir to ensure the Tudor dynasty would continue. Providing an heir would also ensure stability — an unclear succession following a monarch's death had previously led to anarchy, civil war and, in Elizabeth's lifetime, the Lady Jane Grey affair. Marriage was a key method of forging alliances which England sorely needed. The patriarchal society of the time assumed a queen would need a king to support and advise her rule.

Elizabeth was an independent leader who resented the idea of sharing her power with a man or even being expected to follow a man's advice. Elizabeth described naming a successor as being 'buried alive' as it would mean her enemies would develop plots around this successor. There was also the problem of who to choose: Elizabeth could not marry a fellow monarch; foreigners were unpopular in England as seen in the xenophobia leading to Wyatt's Rebellion; marriage to an English noble could create resentment and faction amongst the rest of the nobility; Elizabeth needed to marry a Protestant yet almost all the potential candidates were Catholic. It is also important to remember Elizabeth's personal history — her father's calamitous marriage history, one of which resulted in the execution of her mother, did not make marriage an appealing idea.

Key suitors: Robert Dudley, Earl of Leicester — perhaps Elizabeth's personal preference. He would have been a scandalous choice: his father, brother and grandfather had all been executed as traitors. The rumour surrounding the death of Dudley's wife Amy Robsart in 1560 would have tainted Elizabeth. Dudley's rivals on the Privy Council, primarily Cecil, blocked the marriage on several occasions. Archduke Charles of Austria — promoted by Cecil in 1567 as a key potential ally but his Catholicism was a problem. Francis, Duke of Alencon — the only foreign suitor who came in person to woo Elizabeth, in 1579. He was 23 years younger. Elizabeth was very fond of him. A French alliance was a promising opportunity at a time when Spanish relations were deteriorating. Alencon was not particularly committed to Catholicism. Leicester still used anti-Catholic propaganda to oppose the match. He died in 1584. Now Elizabeth was over 50 there were no more calls to marry.

Despite never naming a successor, Elizabeth's tacit acknowledgement that James VI of Scotland (Mary's son) would be her successor meant the issue was manageable. Elizabeth's letters to James indicated he would be King — this meant he did not oppose his mother's execution in 1587.

facts: Elizabeth was an independent leader who resented the idea of sharing her power with a man. Elizabeth described naming a successor as being 'buried alive' as it would mean her enemies would develop plots around this successor.

Suitors for Elizabeth's hand in marriage: Robert Dudley, Earl of Leicester – perhaps Elizabeth's personal preference. He would have been a scandalous choice. Philip II of Spain – he proposed in 1559 but this would have been a wildly unpopular choice. Archduke Charles of Austria – promoted by Cecil in 1567 as a key potential ally but his Catholicism was a problem. Francis, Duke of Alençon – the only foreign suitor who came in person to woo Elizabeth in 1579, he was extremely charming and Elizabeth was very fond of him despite being 23 years younger than her. Alençon was not particularly committed to Catholicism. He died in 1584.
Parliament repeatedly petitioned Elizabeth to marry or name a successor to no avail. Debates over the issue led to further conflict over parliamentary privilege and freedom of speech.

heading: Impact of the succession question
summary: Elizabeth's refusal to resolve the succession created political instability, fuelled anti-Catholic sentiment and ultimately forced her hand over Mary Queen of Scots.
facts: The succession question was most dangerous in 1562 when Elizabeth nearly died of Smallpox. The Privy Council could not agree on a successor — in desperation Elizabeth asked them to make Robert Dudley Protector of the Realm. The relief from Cecil when Elizabeth recovered demonstrates how deeply the uncertainty about the succession threatened stability.

The next in line to the throne was Elizabeth's cousin Mary, Queen of Scots. If Elizabeth died without a Protestant heir, the Catholic Mary would likely restore Catholicism to England — undoing all of Elizabeth's religious settlement. This gave the succession question constant urgency throughout the reign.

The succession question fuelled conflict between Elizabeth and Parliament. Parliament repeatedly petitioned Elizabeth to marry or name a successor. Elizabeth defended her right not to name a successor as part of the Royal Prerogative. The Wentworth brothers' persistent challenges became a major source of parliamentary conflict.

The 1584 Bond of Association was an unprecedented agreement that anyone who benefited from the assassination of Elizabeth would be killed — in effect ensuring that Mary Queen of Scots would be executed if Elizabeth died. This shows how deeply the question of succession had permeated political life.

Impact on foreign affairs: the ambiguity around the succession was used as a diplomatic tool. Keeping foreign Catholic powers uncertain whether England might become Catholic again under Mary Queen of Scots prevented them from acting aggressively. Philip II of Spain initially supported Elizabeth partly because French-backed Mary QoS was worse from his perspective. Once Mary was executed in 1587 this diplomatic ambiguity disappeared and war with Spain became inevitable.

The impact on relations with Scotland and France: Mary QoS's claim to the English throne gave France a potential lever over England throughout the 1560s and 1570s. Elizabeth's decision to support Scottish Protestant rebels in 1560 (Treaty of Edinburgh) was directly driven by her desire to neutralise the Franco-Scottish threat to her succession. The succession question thus shaped Elizabeth's most significant foreign policy intervention of the early reign.

heading: James VI and the succession
summary: James VI of Scotland was the unspoken heir to Elizabeth's throne — his management by Cecil and his acceptance of his mother's execution made the transition of 1603 possible.
facts: James VI of Scotland was the son of Mary Queen of Scots and Lord Darnley. As Mary's son he was Elizabeth's closest Protestant relative and the most plausible successor to the English throne. Despite Elizabeth never naming him as her heir, it was widely understood from the 1580s onwards that James would succeed her.

James's significance to English politics began with his mother's execution in 1587. Elizabeth and Cecil needed James not to react so aggressively as to provoke a war with Scotland. James protested but ultimately accepted his mother's death — partly because Mary had disinherited him in favour of Philip II of Spain in her will, and partly because he did not want to jeopardise his inheritance of the English crown.

Robert Cecil began a secret correspondence with James from the late 1590s, preparing the ground for a smooth succession. Cecil kept James informed about English politics and reassured him of his likely inheritance. This correspondence was conducted entirely without Elizabeth's knowledge or approval.

James's presence as the likely heir had a stabilising effect on English politics in the later years of Elizabeth's reign — despite the socioeconomic unrest, Essex's rebellion and the costs of war, there was no serious attempt to destabilise the succession. The Protestant gentry and nobility broadly accepted that James was the answer to the succession question.

James became King of England on Elizabeth's death on 24th March 1603, succeeding as James I of England whilst remaining James VI of Scotland. The transition was entirely peaceful — a remarkable achievement given that Elizabeth had never formally named her successor. Cecil's careful management was central to this outcome.

unit: Unit 6 – Financial, Economic and Social Affairs
heading: Financial situation in 1558
summary: Elizabeth inherited a debt of £227,000 from Mary's reign but, with the help of capable administrators, quickly stabilised the finances and paid off the debt by 1576.
facts: When Elizabeth acceded to the throne in 1558, the English Crown had debts of £227,000 left over from Mary's involvement in the war with France. This debt was largely owed to the Antwerp Exchange and came with an interest rate of 14%. It was imperative that Elizabeth cleared these debts as soon as possible.

Mary had introduced some reforms to make financial administration more efficient — most notably the revised Book of Rates which determined customs duties (annual revenue jumped from £29,315 to £82,797 in one year) and gave greater import to the Exchequer which now collected roughly three-quarters of Crown revenue.

Mary's financial administration had been led by two extremely capable figures: Thomas Gresham and William Paulet, whom Elizabeth inherited. Sir Thomas Gresham was a highly perceptive financier who identified three major problems facing Elizabeth's finances: debasement of the coinage begun under Henry VIII; the cost of war and the necessary but damaging loans needed to fund it; and the control the Hanseatic League enjoyed over the export market of English wools from their base at the Steelyard in London, which was damaging English merchants' profits.

Gresham's primary advice to Elizabeth was to maintain an excellent credit rating by swiftly repaying existing debt and avoiding taking loans. This would allow Elizabeth to quickly raise loans at a favourable rate when they became absolutely necessary in times of war. Gresham also argued for usury laws to be relaxed as a stimulus to the English financial markets — Cecil eventually agreed to this in 1571. In 1565 Gresham founded the Royal Exchange as a London equivalent to the Antwerp Exchange.
William Paulet was a highly effective and experienced Lord Treasurer. Despite being in his 70s when Elizabeth came to the throne, he served loyally until his death in 1572, aged 89.

Elizabeth quickly and effectively removed the Marian debt. By 1576 Sir Walter Mildmay informed Parliament that the Marian debt had been removed. By 1584 Elizabeth had accrued a surplus of £300,000. She achieved this by: not indulging in the excessive lifestyle of her father; as a single woman with no children, her household expenditure was smaller; not spending money on lavish building projects, instead going on progress each summer at courtiers' and nobles' expense; and avoiding war at all cost.

unit: Unit 6 – Financial, Economic and Social Affairs
heading: Methods of raising income
summary: Elizabeth relied primarily on ordinary revenue in the first half of her reign, but the war with Spain from 1585 forced increasing dependence on parliamentary taxation.
facts: Ordinary revenue was the income that the Crown would receive by default, every year. Examples included revenue from Crown Lands, Customs Duties, Profits from justice (fines issued as punishment) and Church revenue — for example First Fruits and Tenths.

Extraordinary revenue was income that the Crown could gain in addition to ordinary revenue in times of need. It was not automatically gained and acquisition of it came with potential consequences: parliamentary grants of subsidies could be requested but would allow Parliament to make demands from Elizabeth; loans could be acquired forcibly from wealthy nobles or at high interest rates from financial centres like the Antwerp Exchange or the City of London, but these would alienate the nobles and damage Elizabeth's credit rating.

Crown Lands: Elizabeth increased annual revenues from Crown Lands from £86,000 to £111,000. However this was significantly below the level of inflation. Crown Lands were customarily rented on long leases which meant the short-term, exploitative rent rises employed by members of the nobility were not an option. Elizabeth sold a significant portion of Crown Lands over her reign, bringing in £600,000 but depleting the long-term potential.

Customs Duties: Mary's revision of the Book of Rates in 1558 provided an immediate boost. However whilst inflation continued throughout Elizabeth's reign, the Book of Rates was not regularly revised. Annual revenue from Customs Duties stood at £91,000 in the 1590s — barely an increase from 1558. Elizabeth hoped to increase customs duties by encouraging Englishmen to begin finishing wool into cloth. The reluctance of the English to adopt this new practice limited profits.

Church revenue: Elizabeth gained income from First Fruits and Tenths, profits from recusancy fines — which were increased significantly in 1581 — and by keeping bishoprics vacant for extended periods after the death of a bishop so its revenues defaulted to the Crown.

Parliamentary Taxation: grants came in two forms — a subsidy which raised around £100,000 and the fifteenths and tenths which raised around £30,000. Who would pay what amount was assessed by local gentry — meaning these grants were not as high as possible. They also did not keep pace with inflation. As a result taxes in England were amongst the lowest in Europe.

unit: Unit 6 – Financial, Economic and Social Affairs
heading: Inflation
summary: Inflation was a persistent problem throughout Elizabeth's reign, caused by population growth, poor harvests and Spanish bullion, which the government was unable to fully understand or address.
facts: Inflation had been a problem for every Tudor monarch. Although there had been a decline in inflation by the start of Elizabeth's reign, it accelerated in the 1560s. By the 1560s average food prices were triple what they had been in the reign of Henry VII. Industrial products had approximately doubled. Causes included: population rise — between 1547 and 1603 the population of England increased from c.2.7 million to c.4 million; poor harvests made common by the Little Ice Age; and Bullion — huge quantities of gold and silver arriving in Europe from the New World meant the value of these precious metals decreased and so prices rose.

Sir Thomas Gresham attempted to tackle inflation through recoinage in 1560. The idea was that by replacing debased coins with good ones inflation would ease. By 1561 the debased coins had been called in and the base alloys removed. However prices did not go down — merchants simply set the same prices, or higher.

Elizabeth encouraged her people to limit demand by encouraging fasting during Lent and the observance of 'fish days' on Wednesdays and Fridays. The 1586 Book of Orders prohibited hoarding of grain. Ultimately the lack of understanding of how rising population's impact on supply and demand affected inflation meant the government could not tackle the issue.

Assessments of taxation for parliamentary grants often led to underassessments. This was particularly true for subsidies as the local gentry who made the assessments undervalued their and their lord's lands for their benefit. Elizabeth was reluctant to pay for a professional tax collecting service. Gresham's use of Custom Farmers led to widespread corruption — these officials would make a low estimate of the income they could raise for the Crown and then keep any excesses for themselves.

Even before the outbreak of war with Spain in 1585, the ongoing Dutch Revolt negatively affected English trade. A 1576 mutiny by Spanish troops in Antwerp destroyed much of that city which was a centre for the English wool trade. Elizabeth's seizure of the Genoese Leon in 1568 prompted a trade embargo between England and Spain until 1573.

unit: Unit 6 – Financial, Economic and Social Affairs
heading: The cost of war
summary: The outbreak of war with Spain in 1585 destroyed Elizabeth's financial surplus, costing £4.5 million and forcing reliance on parliamentary taxation, monopolies and the sale of Crown lands.
facts: Even before the outbreak of war with Spain in 1585, the ongoing Dutch Revolt negatively affected English trade. A 1576 mutiny by Spanish troops in Antwerp led to the destruction of much of that city which was a centre for the English wool trade. Elizabeth's seizure of the Genoese Leon in 1568 prompted a trade embargo between England and Spain until 1573. However Spain suffered more from this embargo.

The war did also bring some benefits: many Flemings fled the Netherlands in 1566 and brought improved manufacturing skills to England; Elizabeth's sponsorship of privateers often brought dividends — during his famous circumnavigation of the globe 1577-80 Sir Francis Drake stole large amounts from Spanish ships and ports and a further £140,000 during his 1587 raid on Cadiz.

However it is undoubtedly true that the outbreak of war from 1585 destroyed Elizabeth's finances. The Treaty of Nonsuch committed Elizabeth to £126,000 per year to support the Dutch rebels. In total the war cost £4.5 million — £2 million in the Netherlands, £2 million in Ireland, £500,000 supporting Henry of Navarre and a further £160,000 to defend against the Spanish Armada.

Elizabeth's hard work at improving her finances was made redundant by the war. Her surplus of £300,000 was used almost entirely in the first year. Drake's 'English Armada' of 1589 against Spain was an unmitigated disaster. English attempts to capture the treasure fleet from the New World routinely failed.

Due to the cost of war Elizabeth was forced to resort to monopolies in her later years to reward her courtiers. These contributed to price rises and cause great dissatisfaction. Elizabeth was also forced to sell more Crown Lands in the 1590s, further weakening long-term Royal finances. Despite increased reliance on Parliament for taxation, the War also provided a common enemy around which Crown and Parliament united.

unit: Unit 6 – Financial, Economic and Social Affairs
heading: Overseas trade
summary: Elizabeth sought to diversify English trade beyond the Antwerp cloth market through new trading companies, though the war with Spain severely disrupted commerce.
facts: Prior to Elizabeth's reign English trade had been reliant on the export of wool to the cloth market in Antwerp. However the Dutch Revolt and war with Spain led to the collapse of the Antwerp market and trade embargoes with Spain that severely hampered English trade. Elizabeth needed new markets to replace the Dutch trade and to diversify to ensure England was not reliant on one source of trade.

Northern and Eastern Europe: the Muscovy Company was established in 1555 to trade English wool with Muscovy (Russia) — Russian hides and timber were then imported. However complicated faction and the attitudes of Ivan the Terrible at the Russian court made trade unpredictable and profit limited. In 1579 the Eastland Company was established with a depot in Poland to try to gain a foothold in trade in the Baltic. Traditionally the Hanseatic League dominated trade in the Baltic Sea and so resisted English advances.

The New World: Spain and Portugal dominated the New World, especially the Caribbean and South America. Their dominance made trade impossible and English activity there was limited to piracy. In 1562 Sir John Hawkins created the Triangular Slave Trade by capturing slaves in Sierra Leone and selling them for profit in the Caribbean. Many of the Privy Council and Elizabeth herself sponsored Hawkins on repeat voyages and made substantial profits. Sir Walter Raleigh's attempts to create English colonies in North America on Roanoke Island failed.

The Middle East: in the 1570s English merchants began direct trade with the Mediterranean with silks, spices and olive oil being imported to England. In 1580 the Levant Company was founded to trade with the eastern shores of the Mediterranean, in particular the Ottoman Empire. Attempts to create trade links with the Persian Empire were scuppered by the Shah's unwillingness to trade with non-Muslims.

Asia: a new faster route to the Far East was sought by English merchants hoping to undercut the route dominated by the Portuguese that rounded South Africa. John Davis and Martin Frobisher attempted to find the legendary 'North-West Passage' around the north of North America to the Far East. These were unsuccessful due to adverse weather. In 1600 the East India Company was founded which would trade with India. Whilst it would become hugely important in later centuries, its value was limited in these early years.

unit: Unit 6 – Financial, Economic and Social Affairs
heading: Causes of poverty and vagrancy
summary: Poverty and vagrancy grew throughout Elizabeth's reign due to population growth, enclosure and later the wars with Spain and Ireland, creating widespread social anxiety.
facts: Another consequence of the growing population (rising from 2.8 million in the 1540s to around 4.1 million by Elizabeth's death) was an increase in poverty and vagrancy. A surplus population led to increasing demand for work which allowed employers to lower wages. Simultaneously landlords could raise rents. Combined with wider inflation in the price of goods, this created large amounts of poverty.

In the later years of Elizabeth's reign this was compounded by the wars with Spain and Ireland. Soldiers and sailors were discharged from service at arbitrary locations far from their homes, often with no pay and with serious injuries that prevented them from working.

Contemporaries, who did not understand the impact of the rising population, blamed poverty on greedy landlords and the practice of enclosure. By 1600 in some areas over 70% of the available arable land had been enclosed — though elsewhere this rate was far lower. There is also evidence that enclosure actually declined in Elizabeth's reign as the collapse of the Dutch cloth market removed the gentry's incentive to move from agriculture to sheep farming.

Elizabethans were particularly afraid of vagrants. Ordinary people viewed vagrants as spreaders of disease and criminals who would trick you. The government feared itinerant vagrants encouraged the spread of social unrest. The dominant moral view of the time was that those without work were simply too lazy and should not be helped. These views were all encouraged by pamphlets that spread fear of vagrancy.

The death rate increased by 50% at the peak of the 1595-97 crisis when a series of bad harvests combined with the socioeconomic pressures of war, taxation and population growth. Between 1595-98 there were food riots in Kent, Sussex, Somerset and Norfolk.

unit: Unit 6 – Financial, Economic and Social Affairs
heading: Government responses to poverty
summary: Government attitudes to poverty gradually shifted from punishment towards provision across Elizabeth's reign, culminating in the Poor Law of 1601.
facts: 1563 Statute of Artificers — attempt to increase long-term employment and prevent vagrancy. Introduced compulsory seven-year apprenticeships for craftspeople. JPs set maximum regional wages and discouraged economic migration in search of work. However the Act proved impossible to enforce.

1563 Alms Act — the 'deserving poor' were to be supported by a Poor Rate organised by the Church. Contributions to the Poor Rate were not enforced by the state. 1572 Vagabonds Act — contributions to the Poor Rate made compulsory. Severe penalties enacted against vagrants and the 'undeserving/idle poor' including whipping, mutilation and ultimately execution.

1576 Act for the Relief of the Poor — 'able-bodied' poor would be provided work, often in a House of Correction. First example of the state recognising the 'undeserving poor' also require help, not just punishment. Bridewell in London became the pre-cursor to the House of Correction. Norwich, influenced by the experience of Kett's rebellion, banned begging and instead the wealthiest citizens regularly contributed to a fund to support the poorest. Ipswich, Exeter and Cambridge all introduced similar schemes.

1598 Act for the Relief of the Poor — begging was forbidden suggesting the government's instinct was still to punish the poor. However JPs now appointed materials to employ the able-bodied poor. 1598 Act for the Punishment of Rogues, Vagabonds and Sturdy Beggars — demonstrating that government attitudes to the able-bodied poor had not completely softened, 'sturdy beggars' were to be whipped and returned to their place of birth.
1597 Tillage Act — passed to reverse any enclosure carried out since 1588, indicating the government's acknowledgement that action was needed.

1601 Poor Law — the government assumed the responsibility of providing for the poor from the Church. The distinction between 'deserving' and 'undeserving' poor was codified. Provisions of the 1598 Acts became permanent and would last until the mid-19th century. Many wealthy individuals contributed to the poor by bequeathing funds in their wills. Archbishops Parker and Whitgift contributed to almshouses and Leicester established a hospital for the poor in Warwick.

facts: 1601 Poor Law – the government assumed the responsibility of providing for the Poor Rate from the Church. Provisions of the 1598 Acts became permanent. They would last until the mid-19th century.

Norwich, influenced by the experience of Kett's rebellion, banned begging. Instead the wealthiest citizens regularly contributed to a fund to support the poorest. Ipswich, Exeter and Cambridge all introduced similar schemes.

heading: War with Spain
summary: The war with Spain, officially beginning with the Treaty of Nonsuch in 1585, dominated the later years of Elizabeth's reign, bringing both triumphs like the Armada and enormous financial strain.
facts: War officially began with the Treaty of Nonsuch of 1585 and continued beyond Elizabeth's death until 1604. War was fought in several different theatres: in the Netherlands — Elizabeth sent a force, initially led by Leicester, to support the Dutch rebels against the Spanish; at sea — Elizabeth's Sea Dogs led by Francis Drake attacked Spanish ports in the Spanish Main and attempted to capture the Spanish treasure fleet; in France — Spain and England intervened in the French Wars of Religion where the French Catholic League led by the Duke of Guise fought the Protestant Huguenots led by Henry of Navarre; in Ireland — Spain supported Tyrone's Rebellion with troops.

The most famous event of the war was the defeat of the Spanish Armada — a fearsome invasion force of 130 ships and 57,000 men sent by Philip II to invade England in 1588. Victory was a major propaganda boost for Elizabeth and the Protestant cause. Elizabeth encouraged the belief that God had intervened on her side with a celebratory medal 'God blew, and they were scattered'. Elizabeth's role in the Armada, leading her army in full armour with her famous Tilbury speech, demonstrated her strength and leadership — 'I know I have the body of a weak, feeble woman; but I have the heart and stomach of a king, and of a king of England too.'

This victory came at a huge cost. Prior to the Armada, England's navy was ill-prepared. Whilst Drake's raid on Cadiz delayed the Armada by 12 months, Elizabeth had to raise huge sums to fund her defences — including forced loans totalling £75,000 from the nobility and a further £56,000 at 10% from the corporation of the City of London.

After the Armada, failure was common at sea. Drake's 'English Armada' of 1589 against Spain was an unmitigated disaster. English attempts to capture the treasure fleet routinely failed. However the English capture of the Madre de Dios in 1592 brought riches worth half the Crown's usual annual income. English support for the Dutch rebels ensured their survival and eventual success.

The Huguenot Henry of Navarre's coronation as Henry IV in 1589 seemed a huge opportunity for Elizabeth as a Protestant now sat on the French throne. Elizabeth was desperate to maintain Henry's power and sent him gifts of £20,000 and 10,000 troops. This did have some success until Henry's conversion to Catholicism and unilateral peace with Spain in 1598.

The financial cost: Elizabeth's hard work at improving her finances was made redundant by the war. Her surplus of £300,000 was used almost entirely in the first year. In total the war cost £4.5 million, £2 million of which was spent in Ireland. Elizabeth was forced to sell more Crown Lands in the 1590s and rely on contentious monopolies as a form of patronage. The war also exacerbated faction between the conservative councillors led by Burghley and Robert Cecil and the younger, more hawkish councillors led by Essex.

heading: Parliament in the later years
summary: The war with Spain forced Elizabeth to call Parliament more frequently, giving MPs greater leverage to raise grievances over monopolies, purveyance and the succession.
facts: Prior to 1585 Elizabeth had managed to govern without relying too heavily on Parliament — largely through prudent fiscal management and a pragmatic foreign policy. Elizabeth could even afford to accept 1/3 of a subsidy in 1566 to avoid scrutiny over marriage and the succession. This all changed in 1585 with the outbreak of the war with Spain and the Tyrone Rebellion in Ireland. Five of Elizabeth's ten Parliaments were called after 1585.

Monopolies were a result of Elizabeth's lack of finances in her later years. Since she no longer had funds to bestow lavish gifts on her favourites to maintain loyalty, she resorted instead to granting monopolies. The holder of the monopoly had the sole right to selling that good in England and thus could set the price as they liked — e.g. Essex's monopoly over sweet wines from 1588. Monopolies were raised as a major issue in the Parliament of 1597. In the 1601 Parliament MPs publicly listed the monopolies granted since 1597. One MP sarcastically commented 'is not bread there?'. Elizabeth recognised the need for concessions — she made her Golden Speech to appease MPs' anger and annulled the most contentious monopolies including salt and starch.

Purveyance was the monarch's customary right to purchase goods at lower than market value, especially in times of war. This was a highly contentious issue criticised by MPs in the 1589 and 1593 Parliaments. Burghley and the Privy Council defended purveyance as part of the Royal Prerogative in Parliament and the criticisms were suppressed. Elizabeth privately agreed to investigate the issue but no major concessions were made.

As Elizabeth entered her 60s in the 1590s, Parliament's attention returned to the issue of the succession. Many MPs were concerned that Elizabeth's refusal to name an heir meant that upon Elizabeth's death the throne would pass to a Catholic or cause a civil war. Peter Wentworth MP wrote a pamphlet calling on Parliament to be given the right to examine candidates for the succession. In 1591 Wentworth was questioned by the Privy Council and imprisoned briefly. Prior to the 1593 Parliament he attempted to gain support from other MPs — he was sent to the Tower where he stayed until his death in 1596.

Despite increased tensions the common enemy of Spain helped unite Parliament and Crown. The threat of Spanish invasion increased Parliament's willingness to grant hefty subsidies — in 1589 Parliament granted an unprecedented double subsidy and in 1593 Burghley secured a triple subsidy paid over several years.

facts: Despite Elizabeth's increased reliance on parliament, the War also provided a common enemy around which Crown and Parliament united. In 1589 Parliament granted a double subsidy (twice the usual taxation). Burghley secured a triple subsidy from Parliament in 1593.

heading: Ireland and Tyrone's Rebellion
summary: Ireland was a persistent drain on Elizabeth's resources, culminating in Tyrone's Rebellion of 1594–1603 which cost £2 million to suppress and humiliated Essex.
facts: The English Crown had laid claim to Ireland since the 12th century. By the 16th century, English power was only truly felt in the Pale — the region around Dublin. Beyond the Pale, English authority was weak. Most of Ireland was ruled by local lords who held a large amount of autonomy. Some were Anglo-Norman lords who were sympathetic to English rule. Others were the native Gaelic lords who retained Gaelic culture, the Irish language and Catholicism, and were more resistant to English rule.

Throughout Elizabeth's reign Ireland was a source of unrest which often spilled over into open revolt against the English Crown. The most notable include: the Fitzgerald Rebellions of 1569-73 and 1579-83; and Tyrone's Rebellion 1594-1603 also known as the Nine Years' War. The causes of these rebellions included: the largely independent Gaelic lords resisting the increasing English power in Ireland that threatened their positions; ordinary Irish people hating the arbitrary and brutal rule of the English; and Ireland had remained a Catholic country during the 16th century as English power was too weak to enforce Protestantism.

Elizabeth's unwillingness to commit funds to a comprehensive long-term strategy in Ireland led to a variety of methods poorly-implemented under ever-changing Lord Deputies: Colonisation — in the 1560s the Lord Deputies Sussex and Sidney attempted to create plantations where English Protestant lords were given large swathes of land in Ireland to slowly expand English and Protestant influence; Regional Councils — working with the Gaelic lords failed due to a lack of unity; Conquest — the response of Elizabeth in the face of rebellion which only exacerbated anti-English sentiment.

The most dangerous Irish rebellion was led by Hugh O'Neill, Earl of Tyrone. It was threatening because: it came during the war with Spain which meant Elizabeth's resources were already stretched; Tyrone was able to gain national support across Ireland including from many powerful Irish earls; Tyrone won major victories against the English, most notably at Yellow Ford in 1598 which allowed him to take control of the majority of Ireland; Tyrone was an excellent military leader who utilised his knowledge of the country with guerrilla tactics; in 1599 the Earl of Essex led an English force of 16,000 (the largest force ever sent to Ireland) against Tyrone — he returned home against orders without fighting a battle; from 1601 Philip III of Spain sent troops to support Tyrone — 4,000 Spanish troops landed at Kinsale.

Essex's replacement, Lord Mountjoy, arrived in Ireland in 1600. He conciliated many of the Irish lords and by 1603 had forced Tyrone's surrender days after Elizabeth's death. Tyrone and the other Ulster lords fled to Europe — allowing Ulster to be colonised by Protestants.
In total it cost Elizabeth £2 million to defeat Tyrone's rebellion.

heading: Faction and Essex's rise
summary: Robert Devereux, Earl of Essex, became Elizabeth's favourite in the 1590s, his flamboyant personality and military successes masking his political recklessness and growing rivalry with the Cecils.
facts: Robert Devereux, the Earl of Essex rose to Elizabeth's court as the godson of Leicester and due to his marriage to the daughter of Francis Walsingham. Essex's wit, eloquence and dashing personality quickly made him a favourite of the ageing Elizabeth in the 1590s. Many have speculated that, following Leicester's death in 1588, Essex reminded her of him. In 1593 Essex was raised to the Privy Council, due to his personality more than his political skills.

On the Privy Council, Essex's flamboyant arrogance often clashed with the more pragmatic and capable Lord Burghley and his son, Robert Cecil. Essex frequently acted unilaterally in the War with Spain: in 1589 Essex joined Drake's English Armada against Elizabeth's direct orders; in 1592 Essex disobeyed orders to confer with Henry IV of France without Elizabeth's permission; Essex's capture of Cadiz in 1596 made him extremely popular across England.

In the 1590s, following Leicester's death and due to Burghley's dotage, both Essex and Robert Cecil competed to be the principal figure on the Privy Council. Both strived to get their supporters roles in the Council. In 1596, during Essex's expedition to Cadiz, Robert Cecil became Elizabeth's Secretary of State, thus securing control over the government.

During discussions over how to deal with Tyrone's Rebellion, Essex reacted angrily to suggestions that Mountjoy should command — he feared that in his absence he would lose further power to Cecil. Petulantly he turned his back on Elizabeth, an action of defiance which resulted in a public slap from the Queen. Essex then half-drew his sword in a dangerous show of defiance — but he did go to Ireland.

In Ireland in 1599, Essex was a failure. He led the largest force ever sent to Ireland (16,000 men) and his army far outnumbered Tyrone's. Despite this, Essex never fought a battle and returned to London without permission. Essex's defiant return enraged Elizabeth and Essex was placed under house arrest.

heading: Essex's Rebellion
summary: Essex's disastrous Irish campaign and subsequent house arrest led to a desperate and poorly planned rebellion in 1601 that was quickly crushed.
facts: Whilst in house arrest, Essex's reputation declined even further. First he lost his monopoly over sweet wines — his main source of income. Then the success of Lord Mountjoy in crushing the Tyrone Rebellion further disgraced Essex.

In desperation to reclaim his former position, Essex began his 1601 rebellion. Essex gathered a band of supporters and sympathisers in the City of London — this included the capable Earl of Southampton. He made contact with James VI of Scotland, attempting to become James's key advisor following Elizabeth's planned deposition. He controversially commissioned a performance of Shakespeare's Richard II which ends with a childless monarch being deposed by a noble to save the country from misrule. Elizabeth had banned this play.
The next day Essex attempted to raise a rebellion and seize control. Most of his supporters got cold feet and did not materialise — the rebellion was quickly defeated.
Essex and just five supporters were executed for treason in 1601. From then on, Cecil's faction controlled government unopposed.

subheadings.label: Background
facts: During discussions over how to deal with Tyrone's Rebellion, Essex reacted angrily to suggestions that Mountjoy should command — he expected the position himself. He was sent to Ireland with 16,000 men but never fought a battle, made an unauthorised truce with Tyrone and returned to London without permission.
Essex's defiant return enraged Elizabeth and Essex was placed under house arrest. His humiliation was compounded when Lord Mountjoy was sent to Ireland and succeeded where Essex had failed.

Whilst in house arrest, Essex lost his monopoly over sweet wines — his main source of income. He controversially commissioned a performance of Shakespeare's Richard II, which depicted the deposition of a weak and childless monarch. Elizabeth had banned the play. Essex commented 'I am Richard II, know ye not that?'

subheadings.label: Events and failure
facts: In desperation to reclaim his former position, Essex gathered a band of supporters in London including the Earl of Southampton. On 8 February 1601, he led them into the City of London hoping to raise popular rebellion against Cecil's dominance. Most of his supporters got cold feet — the rebellion was almost immediately defeated.

Essex and just five supporters were executed for treason in 1601. From then on, Robert Cecil's faction controlled government unopposed. Cecil managed the smooth transition of power to James VI of Scotland in 1603 — secretly corresponding with James throughout the final years of Elizabeth's reign.

heading: Socioeconomic unrest in the 1590s
summary: A series of bad harvests from 1594–1598 combined with the costs of war and taxation created serious social unrest in the 1590s, culminating in the Oxfordshire Rising of 1596.
facts: Despite efforts to manage the problem earlier in her reign, inflation persisted into the end of Elizabeth's reign. A series of bad harvests from 1594-1598 led to the average price of wheat doubling. Cheaper grains like oats or rye increased at an even faster rate which inordinately affected the poorest in society. The lack of government action and effective transportation meant that grains could not be moved from areas with surplus to areas with deficit. At the peak of this crisis in 1595-7, the death rate increased by 50%.

Plague: poorer nutrition weakens the immune system of the population and so plague spread easily in 1596-7. Books of Orders were issued to attempt localised quarantines but these were often ignored or not understood. Tax burden: during the War with Spain parliament approved unprecedented levels of taxation in 1589 and 1593. Tax collectors often were unwilling to accurately tax the nobility or gentry for fear of losing their positions and so over-exploited the people. Elizabeth's granting of monopolies to her favourites in the latter years often increased prices on staple goods.

Food shortages and poverty led to periodic unrest throughout the 1590s. Between 1595-98 there were food riots in Kent, Sussex, Somerset and Norfolk. The most notable example was the Oxfordshire Rising of 1596 — ostensibly a protest against enclosure but came at the peak of the food crisis of the mid 1590s. Supposedly the plot was to tear down enclosures, gather arms and march on London. The plot was betrayed to the government who quickly cracked down to make an example — the five ringleaders were publicly tried and executed as traitors in London. In the end the plot was never that serious — only four actually turned up for the plan.

1597 Tillage Act — passed to reverse any enclosure carried out since 1588. 1598 Act for the Relief of the Poor — begging was forbidden but JPs now appointed materials to employ the able-bodied poor. 1598 Act for the Punishment of Rogues, Vagabonds and Sturdy Beggars — 'sturdy beggars' were to be whipped and returned to their place of birth. 1601 Poor Law — the government assumed the responsibility of providing for the poor from the Church. The distinction between 'deserving' and 'undeserving' poor was codified. Provisions lasted until the mid-19th century.

subheadings.label: Causes
facts: Despite efforts to manage the problem earlier in her reign, inflation persisted into the end of Elizabeth's reign. A series of bad harvests from 1594–98 led to the average price of wheat doubling. Cheaper grains like oats and rye increased in price at an even faster rate. At the peak of the crisis in 1595–97 the death rate increased by 50%.

During the war with Spain, Parliament approved unprecedented levels of taxation in 1589 and 1593. Tax collectors found it increasingly difficult to collect the full amount as the population was unable to pay. Elizabeth's granting of monopolies to her favourites often increased prices on staple goods.

Government action: the 1597 Tillage Act was passed to reverse any enclosure carried out since 1588. The 1598 Acts for the Relief of the Poor and Punishment of Rogues strengthened poor relief. The 1601 Poor Law formalised the system, making the state permanently responsible for the poor — provisions that lasted until the mid-19th century.

subheadings.label: Events
facts: Food shortages and poverty led to widespread unrest. Between 1595–98 there were food riots in Kent, Sussex, Somerset and Norfolk. Bands of roving unemployed men, many of them discharged soldiers, further threatened order.

The most notable example was the Oxfordshire Rising of 1596 — ostensibly a protest against enclosure, it came at the peak of the food crisis. The plot was discovered and the five ringleaders were publicly tried and executed as traitors. In the end only four people actually turned up — suggesting the threat of unrest was greater than the actual unrest.

subheadings.label: Government response
facts: Local responses were often more innovative than central government — Norwich, influenced by the experience of Kett's rebellion, had banned begging and created a community fund. The contrast between effective local action and sluggish central response revealed the structural limits of Elizabethan government.

heading: Elizabeth's reputation
summary: Elizabeth carefully managed her public image through portraiture and pageantry, though in her final years scandal at court and socioeconomic problems undermined the myth of Gloriana.
facts: As with other monarchs, Elizabeth's power relied on her image. It was important that Elizabeth seemed strong and divinely ordained to symbolise stability and to prevent anxiety over the succession creating potential factional struggles. Annual Accession Day Tilts on November 17 were lavishly celebrated to honour Elizabeth's virtues and portray her court as the apex of chivalry and loyalty.

As Elizabeth entered her 60s her looks diminished. Her fondness for sugar had blackened her teeth. Her grey hair was hidden by a bright red wig that was often mocked by younger courtiers. Her face, pockmarked from the Smallpox she had contracted in 1562, was always heavily made-up with white lead paint. To maintain the outward image of strength and stability, in her official portraits Elizabeth still appeared as young as in her coronation in 1558.

In 1596 the Privy Council ordered the destruction of any 'unseemly and improper' portraits of Elizabeth. All portraits had to be based on an agreed, flattering version of Elizabeth's face produced by Nicholas Hilliard. Portraits like the Rainbow Portrait used heavy symbology to enhance Elizabeth's image — she holds a rainbow, a symbol of peace and divine favour. On her dress are eyes and ears showing that Elizabeth sees and hears all — no one can plot against her.

A series of scandals undermined Elizabeth's image at court — for example Walter Raleigh's disgrace at making Bess Throckmorton (one of Elizabeth's closest ladies) pregnant. Attendance at court tailed off and the nobility were sometimes reluctant to accompany Elizabeth on progress. Elizabeth herself withdrew into her chambers more and more. However every year on November 17 Accession Day Tilts were lavishly celebrated. Works like Edmund Spenser's poem The Faerie Queene that glorified Elizabeth's image were widely read.

Elizabeth continued to travel the country on progress every summer allowing more of her people to see her. However some reported her looking 'old and ill'. The socioeconomic unrest of the 1590s led to increased popular criticism of a Queen who seemingly was doing little to help. Some commented 'We shall never have a merry world while the queen liveth'.

In her final Parliament of 1601, Elizabeth made her famous Golden Speech where she reduced many MPs to tears as she evoked her love for England and her subjects. It was seen as a glorious end of an era.

unit: Chapter 1 – Origins of the Cold War to 1945
heading: Opposing ideologies
summary: The Cold War was rooted in the fundamental incompatibility of capitalism and communism as economic and political systems.
facts: The heart of the Cold War is the clash of ideologies between Communism and Capitalism. Communism: policy that the state should own all property and industry to ensure every citizen has a fair share — based on the writings of Marx. Capitalism: policy that everyone should be free to own property and businesses, with competition in markets essential to a country's success.

The main intellectual basis of communism was constructed in the nineteenth century by Friedrich Engels and Karl Marx. Marx argued that capitalism would inevitably be overthrown by the workers in a socialist revolution, leading eventually to a true egalitarian Communist society. Lenin developed Marx's ideas for Russian conditions — founding the Bolshevik Party in 1903, which seized power in October 1917.

Under Lenin and then Stalin, the USSR became an authoritarian Communist state where the government was in charge of all aspects of the economy, there were no democratic elections and freedom of speech was limited. The state did not 'wither away' as Marx had predicted.

For the West, democracy meant the liberty of the individual, equality before the law, freedom of speech and a parliament elected by the people. The USSR dismissed parliamentary democracy as a mere camouflage for capitalism. For Marxist-Leninists, democracy meant economic equality with no extremes of wealthy capitalists and poor workers.

Marxism-Leninism was opposed to religion — 'the opium of the masses'. During the revolution in Russia, churches, mosques and synagogues were closed down and religion was banned. In Europe, Christian Churches were among the leading critics of communism.

The USSR had been communist since the 1917 revolution. Capitalist America had seen the Red Scare in the 1920s and 1930s. These deep ideological differences meant that even when the two sides cooperated against Nazi Germany, fundamental tensions remained.

subheadings.label: Communism
facts: Communism was constructed by Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels in the 19th century. Marx argued capitalism would inevitably be overthrown by the workers (proletariat) in a socialist revolution, leading eventually to a classless, equal society.

Lenin developed Marx's ideas for Russia in the early 20th century, founding the Bolshevik Party in 1903, which seized power in October 1917. Under Lenin and then Stalin, the USSR became an authoritarian state with no democratic elections and limited freedom of speech.

subheadings.label: Capitalism
facts: Capitalism is an economic system based on private investment and profit. The West believed in the liberty of the individual, equality before the law, freedom of speech and elected government.
The USSR dismissed parliamentary democracy as a camouflage for capitalism. For Marxist-Leninists, democracy meant economic equality under the dictatorship of the proletariat.

subheadings.label: Why they were incompatible
facts: Marxism-Leninism was opposed to religion — Marx called it 'the opium of the masses'. During the Russian Revolution, churches, mosques and synagogues were closed down and religion was banned.

In the West, Christian Churches were among the leading enemies of communism. In 1979 the election of Pope John Paul II of Poland as head of the Roman Catholic Church strengthened political opposition to communism in Poland.

unit: Chapter 1 – Origins of the Cold War to 1945
heading: Long-term tensions 1917–1941
summary: Deep mutual suspicion between the capitalist West and communist USSR pre-dated the Cold War by over two decades.
facts: The Bolshevik Revolution of 1917 and the subsequent Civil War (1919-22) immediately created tension with the West. Western powers including Britain, France and the USA had intervened on the side of the anti-Bolshevik Whites during the Civil War. The USSR never forgot this.

Key tensions in the 1920s and 1930s included: Soviet refusal to honour debts owed by the previous Russian government; Soviet nationalisation of the economy causing loss of foreign investment; the 1920s Red Scare in the USA; the 1919-21 Polish-Soviet War; and Soviet show trials and oppression in the 1930s.

In 1938 Western powers pursued a policy of Appeasement, signing the Munich Agreement which ceded part of Czechoslovakia to Hitler. The USSR was not consulted. Stalin interpreted this as the West allowing Hitler to expand eastwards — potentially towards the USSR.

In 1939 Stalin signed the Nazi-Soviet Pact — a non-aggression agreement with Hitler. This shocked the West and allowed Hitler to invade Poland in September 1939, starting World War Two. Stalin used the time to absorb Latvia, Lithuania and Estonia.

Operation Barbarossa — the Nazi invasion of the Soviet Union in June 1941 — transformed the situation. The Soviets were caught by surprise and quickly in full retreat. Stalin was desperate — only the vast size of the Soviet Union prevented a German victory.

Churchill was quick to see the potential of Soviet might in Britain's war with Germany. The USSR's image was transformed in the West from a brutal dictatorship to that of patriots bravely resisting the Nazis, led by 'Uncle Joe' as Stalin came to be known. The Grand Alliance was formed out of necessity.

subheadings.label: The revolution and its impact
facts: The Bolshevik Revolution of October 1917 alarmed Western powers — Britain, the USA, France and Japan had all intervened in Russia's Civil War (1917–22) on the side of the Whites against the communist Reds.
The establishment of the Comintern in 1919 — an international organisation to promote communism — confirmed Western fears that the USSR sought to export revolution.

The 1920s and 1930s saw a 'Red Scare' in the USA as fear of communist infiltration grew. The USSR's nationalisation of the economy led to loss of foreign investment and Soviet refusal to honour debts owed by previous Russian governments.

subheadings.label: Interwar tensions
facts: Stalin's show trials and oppression in the 1930s reinforced Western perceptions of the USSR as a brutal dictatorship. The 1938 Munich Agreement (Western appeasement of Hitler) convinced Stalin that the West wanted Germany and Russia to fight each other.
The Nazi-Soviet Pact of August 1939 shocked the West — it seemed to confirm that communism and fascism had more in common than communism and democracy.

subheadings.label: The Nazi-Soviet Pact
facts: Operation Barbarossa in June 1941 transformed relations — Churchill was quick to see the potential of Soviet might and forged the Grand Alliance. The USSR's image was transformed in the West from a brutal dictatorship to patriots bravely resisting the Nazis, led by 'Uncle Joe' Stalin.

unit: Chapter 1 – Origins of the Cold War to 1945
heading: Wartime tensions in the Grand Alliance
summary: Despite their alliance against Hitler, the USA, USSR and Britain were divided by the second front, Poland and their competing visions for post-war Europe.
facts: Since 1941 the USSR, USA and UK had been united in a Grand Alliance against the common enemy of Nazism. However this alliance had tensions from the start: Churchill was highly anti-Communist and suspicious of Stalin's intentions in Eastern Europe; Roosevelt was also suspicious of Stalin but was equally suspicious of Churchill's imperial ambitions; Stalin was resentful to the UK and US for delaying their invasion of Nazi-occupied territory until 1944.

The Atlantic Charter (August 1941) was a joint British and American document affirming their war aims — self-determination and internal political, economic and religious freedom. It was endorsed by 126 countries including the USSR, although they were not part of writing it. This demonstrated a severe threat to Soviet ideas about how societies should be organised.

The Second Front: the USSR proposed that the Allies create a Second Front through France. They felt they had been fighting the bulk of the war in Europe alone while the Western Allies defended territories in North Africa. Churchill wanted the Second Front to be opened in the Balkans to prevent Soviet influence there. Britain and the USA stalled for several years — causing Stalin to doubt their commitment to Soviet security. The Second Front finally opened in June 1944.

Poland was deeply divisive. Poland's geographical position made it vital strategic territory for the USSR — it had been invaded via Poland three times. Britain was hosting the Polish government in exile (the London Poles) hoping to restore them to power. The West wanted a free and democratic government; the USSR saw it as a vital buffer zone. This fundamental disagreement would run from 1943 to Potsdam.

Churchill's Percentages Agreement with Stalin in October 1944 — in which Churchill proposed dividing Eastern Europe into spheres of influence (e.g. 90% British influence in Greece, 90% Soviet influence in Romania) — showed that Britain was willing to accept Soviet dominance in some areas. Roosevelt was not consulted and did not approve.

When Roosevelt died in April 1945 he was replaced by Harry Truman, who was far more hostile to Stalin. At Potsdam, Attlee replaced Churchill as British Prime Minister mid-conference after Labour won the 1945 general election. These changes weakened the personal relationships that had held the Grand Alliance together — Truman had no trust in Stalin and was far less willing to compromise.

unit: Chapter 1 – Origins of the Cold War to 1945
heading: Relations between the Big Three
summary: The personal relationships between the leaders of the Grand Alliance were central to its functioning — and their deterioration helps explain the breakdown into Cold War.
facts: Stalin, Roosevelt and Churchill — the Big Three — had very different personalities and aims. Roosevelt was optimistic about post-war cooperation and believed he could manage Stalin personally. Churchill was deeply suspicious of Soviet intentions and wanted to limit Soviet influence in Eastern Europe. Stalin was determined to secure the USSR's borders and create a buffer zone — he had seen his country invaded twice in twenty years.

Roosevelt and Churchill had a close relationship built on the Atlantic Charter (1941) and their shared war aims. However they disagreed fundamentally on strategy — Churchill wanted to open the Second Front in the Balkans to limit Soviet influence, whilst Roosevelt sided with Stalin in insisting on a French invasion. This disagreement weakened the Western position.

Churchill's Percentages Agreement with Stalin (October 1944) — in which Eastern Europe was divided into spheres of influence — showed Churchill's pragmatic acceptance of Soviet power in the East in exchange for Western dominance in Greece. Roosevelt was not consulted and disapproved of this imperial-style division.

Roosevelt's death in April 1945 fundamentally changed the dynamic. Truman was far more hostile to Stalin than Roosevelt and had no personal rapport with him. Truman was outraged by Soviet actions in Poland and made this clear at Potsdam. Stalin found Truman far harder to manage than Roosevelt.

At Potsdam, Churchill was replaced mid-conference by Clement Attlee after Labour won the British general election. Attlee was less familiar to Stalin and less forceful in standing up to Soviet demands. The change of British leadership at such a critical moment weakened Western continuity.

By Potsdam the personal bonds of the Grand Alliance had dissolved. The common enemy of Nazism was gone. Truman had the atomic bomb and was not afraid to use it as leverage. Stalin had broken his promises over Poland. The personal relationships that might have smoothed over ideological differences had been replaced by mutual suspicion and hostility.

heading: The Tehran Conference 1943
summary: The first meeting of the Big Three in November 1943 — the most cooperative of the wartime conferences, focused on strategy rather than the post-war world.
facts: The Big Three (Stalin, Roosevelt, Churchill) met for the first time in Tehran in November 1943. The war was still far from won — the main aims of the conference were to direct wartime strategy rather than plan the post-war world.

unit: Chapter 1 – Origins of the Cold War to 1945
heading: The Yalta Conference 1945
summary: Yalta (February 1945) was the high point of Allied cooperation — but the vague agreements on Poland and Eastern Europe contained the seeds of future conflict.
facts: Yalta, February 1945 (Roosevelt, Stalin, Churchill): by Yalta it was clear the Nazis would lose the war — attention shifted to the post-war world. Agreed: Germany to be split into four occupation zones; Berlin also split; Germany to pay $20 billion in reparations, half to the USSR; the United Nations to be established.

Stalin promised free elections in Eastern Europe. Eastern Europe would be a Soviet sphere of influence — though this was never clearly defined. Stalin wanted greater UN representation for individual Soviet republics, fearing it would become anti-Soviet.

Poland was deeply disputed. The West wanted to assure a free and democratic government — Britain had gone to war to uphold Polish independence and was hosting the government in exile (the London Poles). The USSR saw Poland as a vital buffer zone. There was little to guarantee Stalin would deliver free elections.

Yalta was the high point of Allied cooperation — but free elections and sphere of influence meant completely different things to Stalin and to the West. The vague language of Yalta contained the seeds of future conflict.

unit: Chapter 1 – Origins of the Cold War to 1945
heading: The Potsdam Conference
summary: Potsdam revealed a dramatic escalation of tension — the common enemy was defeated, Roosevelt was dead, and the atomic bomb had been used without telling Stalin.
facts: Potsdam, July-August 1945 (Truman, Stalin, Attlee): after the defeat of the Nazis. The war with Japan continued. By Potsdam tensions had increased significantly — Hitler's death had removed the common enemy.

The personal dynamics had shifted dramatically. Roosevelt's death changed the relationship — Truman was far more hostile to Stalin and had no personal rapport with him. Between Yalta and Potsdam Stalin had set up a communist puppet government in Poland, breaking his promise of free elections. Attlee replaced Churchill mid-conference after Labour won the British general election — the change of leaders weakened Western continuity.

America's atomic bomb increased tensions enormously. Truman informed Stalin that the USA had a new weapon of unusual destructive force. Stalin already knew through espionage and simply said he hoped America would make good use of it. Stalin felt very vulnerable — he was not informed of the bomb's use on Japan until after the fact, which he saw as a direct threat.
Agreed: Germany to be divided as agreed at Yalta; reparations to be taken from each zone as decided by the occupier; the UN to be set up; Nazi war criminals to be tried.

Disagreed: Britain and America did not want to implement harsh reparations on Germany — they feared a repeat of Versailles and wanted Germany to recover as a buffer against Communism. Stalin, who had lost 25 million men in the war, wanted very harsh reparations. Truman strongly objected to the Soviet presence in Eastern Europe and the lack of free elections.

unit: Chapter 1 – Origins of the Cold War to 1945
heading: Liberation of Europe — East vs West
summary: The different ways East and West liberated Europe from Nazi rule created fundamentally different political realities that deepened Cold War division.
facts: Allied Control Commissions (ACCs) were set up in each occupied territory after liberation, including Germany. There was a precedent that the country which had done the bulk of the liberating had more sway on the ACC. The first ACC was set up in Italy in 1943 — as the USSR had not had troops there, it was not represented.

Similarly, the Soviets dominated the ACCs in Romania, Bulgaria, Finland and Hungary — countries they had liberated. This gave them enormous practical power to shape the post-war settlement in Eastern Europe.

Partisan groups (resistance fighters fighting to liberate their own country) could also influence the post-war settlement. Yugoslavia and Albania liberated themselves via partisan forces led by Tito and Hoxha — and consequently enjoyed more freedom after the war. Poland liberated itself with the London Poles but was undermined by Soviet interference.

The USSR had liberated Eastern Europe from Nazi rule. Now Stalin sought to turn these states into a buffer zone to protect the USSR from any future invasion. Latvia, Lithuania and Estonia were absorbed into the USSR. Hungary, Poland, Romania, Bulgaria, Czechoslovakia and Albania became communist one-party states with the help of the Red Army between 1945-8.

Yugoslavia, whilst communist, resisted Stalin and maintained independence under Tito. In June 1948 Yugoslavia was expelled from Cominform after Tito refused to submit to Soviet direction. After 1948 the Soviet Union broke off diplomatic relations with Tito.

In 1946 Churchill declared an Iron Curtain had descended over Europe — dividing it between the capitalist West and communist East. The different experiences of liberation directly determined which side of the Iron Curtain countries would fall.

subheadings.label: Western liberation
facts: Allied Control Commissions (ACCs) were set up in each occupied territory. The precedent was that the country which had done the bulk of the 'liberating' had more sway on the ACC — so the USSR dominated ACCs in Romania, Bulgaria, Finland and Hungary.

Western liberation: in France, the Low Countries and Denmark, Allied forces were seen as liberators, bringing supplies. There was no thought of annexing territory or imposing an ideology. The situation was more complex in Greece, where Britain supported royalists in a civil war to prevent a communist state.

subheadings.label: Eastern liberation
facts: Eastern liberation: the Red Army inflicted much harsher retribution on Germany and its allies — there were terrible reprisals against civilians, widespread plunder and deportation of ethnic Germans. In annexed territories, pre-1918 Russian territories were restored to Soviet control.

Soviet political influence: the Russian forces were deeply involved in the politics of liberated countries. They supported a communist coup in Romania (1945), installed a communist-dominated coalition in Hungary, controlled Bulgaria via a Special Allied Control Council and established a National Liberation Committee in Poland dominated by communists.

By 1948, Latvia, Lithuania and Estonia had been absorbed into the USSR. Hungary, Poland, Romania, Bulgaria, Czechoslovakia and Albania had all become communist one-party states with the help of the Red Army. Yugoslavia, though communist, resisted Stalin and maintained independence under Tito.

subheadings.label: Consequences
facts: In 1946, Churchill declared an 'Iron Curtain' had descended across Europe — dividing the free West from the Soviet-dominated East.

unit: Chapter 2 – Development of the Cold War 1946–1955
heading: The creation of the United Nations
summary: The UN was created in 1945 as an international peacekeeping organisation, but immediately became a battleground for Cold War tensions.
facts: The United Nations was established in 1945, replacing the failed League of Nations. Roosevelt had convinced the USSR to join — it was seen as a key tool for maintaining post-war peace through collective security.

The UN Security Council had five permanent members with veto power: the USA, USSR, UK, France and China. The USSR could use its veto to block any resolution it disagreed with — making the UN immediately a Cold War battleground.

The UN was immediately undermined by Cold War tensions. The USSR used its veto repeatedly to block Western proposals. The USA and its allies had a majority in the General Assembly — making the UN appear as an instrument of American foreign policy to the Soviets.

During the Korean War (1950-53) the UN authorised military action against North Korea because the USSR was temporarily boycotting the Security Council over China's representation. This was the only time the UN directly intervened militarily against Soviet-backed forces.

Despite its limitations, the UN provided a forum for dialogue and a mechanism for managing crises. It played a role in mediating disputes and providing humanitarian aid. The establishment of the UN reflected the shared hope in 1945 that a new international order could prevent another world war.

subheadings.label: What the UN was
facts: The United Nations was established on 24 October 1945, replacing the ineffective League of Nations which had failed to prevent WWII. Its headquarters were in Manhattan, New York City, reflecting the rise of the United States to global leadership.

The Security Council was the UN's most powerful body — the five permanent members (USA, USSR, UK, France and China) each had the power of veto. This immediately gave the USSR the ability to block any measure it disagreed with.

subheadings.label: Immediate Cold War battleground
facts: At its first meeting in 1946, the Security Council immediately became a Cold War arena. Iran raised the matter of Russian-occupied Azerbaijan; Russia countered by opening the issue of British troops in Greece. Russia used the first Security Council veto to block a plan for Britain and France to withdraw from Syria and Lebanon.

The Atomic Control Commission was created at the first UN meeting to 'deal with problems raised by the discovery of atomic energy'. The USA proposed international control of atomic weapons; the USSR rejected this as they did not yet have their own bomb and feared American dominance.

subheadings.label: Assessment
facts: Stalin had insisted on greater representation for individual Soviet republics in the UN, fearing it would become anti-Soviet. He eventually won representation for Ukraine and Byelorussia as separate members alongside the USSR.

Despite the Cold War tensions, the UN provided a forum for diplomacy and debate that helped prevent direct superpower conflict. It played a role in the Korean War (1950–53) when the USSR was boycotting the Security Council and the USA was able to pass a resolution authorising military action.

unit: Chapter 2 – Development of the Cold War 1946–1955
heading: The Iron Curtain speech and its significance
summary: Churchill's Iron Curtain speech of March 1946 gave voice to Western fears about Soviet expansionism and helped harden attitudes on both sides.
facts: In March 1946 Winston Churchill gave his Iron Curtain speech at Fulton, Missouri, USA — with President Truman present. Churchill declared: 'From Stettin in the Baltic to Trieste in the Adriatic, an iron curtain has descended across the Continent.'

Churchill warned that the Soviet Union did not want war but did want the fruits of war and the indefinite expansion of its power and doctrines. He called for an Anglo-American alliance to confront Soviet expansion.
Stalin reacted furiously, comparing Churchill to Hitler and calling the speech a call for war against the USSR. The Soviet press attacked Churchill as a warmonger.

The speech was significant because it publicly named the division of Europe and gave it the iconic phrase 'Iron Curtain'. It helped shift Western public opinion against the USSR and made the Cold War visible to ordinary people for the first time.

However its accuracy was debated — in 1946 Soviet control of Eastern Europe was still incomplete. In Czechoslovakia, for example, there had been free elections in 1946 that the Communists won with only 38% of the vote. Full Soviet control was not consolidated until 1948.

subheadings.label: What Churchill said
facts: In March 1946, Churchill made a speech in Fulton, Missouri, calling it 'The Sinews of Peace'. He coined the famous phrase: 'From Stettin in the Baltic to Trieste in the Adriatic, an iron curtain has descended across the continent.'

Key ideas in the speech: Europe was firmly divided; the USSR controlled all Eastern European countries equally; the West needed to negotiate from a position of strength; the USSR wanted to expand without limit and to export communism.
Churchill's key ideas: Stalin was admiring of strength and despising of weakness — the West must deal with him 'supported by the whole strength of the English-speaking world'.

subheadings.label: Reactions
facts: Reactions: Stalin reacted by accusing Churchill of being 'a firebrand of war' and arguing the USSR had only peaceful ambitions. Many in the USA thought the speech was irresponsible. Truman did not immediately signify his approval.

subheadings.label: Accuracy and significance
facts: The speech's accuracy was flawed — Soviet influence was not yet uniform across Eastern Europe. Berlin was not under total Soviet control; total Soviet domination was not yet established in Prague; Yugoslavia under Tito was resisting Moscow.

Despite its inaccuracies, the vivid image of the speech helped to encourage anti-Russian sentiment and provoked equally strong rhetoric from the USSR, ramping up tension and verbal conflict. By 1946 the mood in the USA was shifting away from isolationism to opposing communist expansion.

unit: Chapter 2 – Development of the Cold War 1946–1955
heading: Soviet control of Eastern Europe — salami tactics
summary: Between 1945 and 1948, the USSR used salami tactics to install communist governments across Eastern Europe, turning it into a Soviet buffer zone.
facts: Stalin used so-called salami tactics to take control of Eastern Europe — slicing away opposition piece by piece. The method combined rigged elections, political intimidation, the merging of socialist and communist parties, and the use of the Red Army's presence as a threat.

The Baltic States — Latvia, Lithuania and Estonia — were directly absorbed into the USSR itself (not made satellite states) in 1940 during the Nazi-Soviet Pact, and again after 1945. They lost their independent governments entirely and became Soviet republics. Their populations were subject to mass deportations to Siberia.

Key Eastern European examples: Poland — January 1947, rigged elections gave Communists 80% of the vote; Romania — December 1947, King Michael forced to abdicate; Bulgaria — opposition leaders arrested and executed; Hungary — the Communist party won only 17% in 1945 free elections but by 1947 had taken full control through intimidation of the minister of the interior.

Czechoslovakia was the most significant case. In May 1946 free elections saw the Communist party win 38% — they were part of a coalition. In February 1948, with Soviet backing, the Communists staged a coup and took full control. This event shocked the West and directly prompted Congress to approve Marshall Aid.

Greece was the exception — it remained in the Western sphere. Churchill's Percentages Agreement with Stalin in October 1944 had given Britain 90% influence there. A civil war broke out between communists and the Greek government. Stalin largely respected the Percentages Agreement and did not directly support the Greek communists — though Yugoslavia's Tito did, against Stalin's wishes.

Yugoslavia, whilst communist, resisted Stalin and maintained independence under Tito. Yugoslavia had liberated itself via partisan forces and so had not been occupied by the Red Army. In 1948 Yugoslavia was expelled from Cominform after Tito refused to submit to Soviet direction. After 1948, Tito-ism (the idea that national communist parties should be independent of the USSR) became a feared heresy in the Eastern bloc.
