heading: Espionage in the Cold War
summary: Espionage was central to Cold War rivalry — from atomic secrets passed to the Soviets in the 1940s to moles buried deep in Western intelligence agencies for decades.
facts: Klaus Fuchs was a German-born British physicist who worked on the Manhattan Project and passed detailed atomic weapons designs to the Soviet Union. His intelligence significantly accelerated the Soviet bomb programme — the USSR tested its first atomic weapon in 1949, years earlier than the West expected. Fuchs was convicted of espionage in 1950 and sentenced to 14 years in prison.

The Rosenbergs: Julius and Ethel Rosenberg were American citizens convicted of passing atomic secrets — including information from Fuchs's contacts in the US — to the Soviet Union. Executed in June 1953, they were the first US civilians to be put to death for espionage. Their case inflamed McCarthyism and domestic anti-communist hysteria in the USA.

The Cambridge Five were five British intelligence officers recruited by Soviet intelligence at Cambridge University in the 1930s: Kim Philby, Guy Burgess, Donald Maclean, Anthony Blunt and John Cairncross. They passed British and American intelligence to the USSR for decades. Philby — the most damaging — was head of the anti-Soviet section of MI6. He fled to Moscow in 1963 after being exposed. The Cambridge Five showed the depth of Soviet penetration of Western intelligence.

Aldrich Ames was a CIA officer who began spying for the Soviet Union in 1985. He revealed the identities of virtually every Soviet source working for the CIA — resulting in at least ten executions. He was arrested in 1994. Ames was motivated primarily by money rather than ideology, demonstrating how espionage persisted into the later Cold War.

The U-2 incident (1960): a US U-2 spy plane was shot down over Soviet territory on 1 May 1960. Eisenhower refused to apologise, admitting to Soviet overflights. Khrushchev used the incident to walk out of the Paris Summit and cancel Eisenhower's visit to Moscow — demonstrating how espionage directly damaged diplomacy.

Gunter Guillaume was the personal aide to West German Chancellor Willy Brandt — revealed in 1974 to be a Stasi spy for East Germany. His exposure forced Brandt to resign, ending the political career of the architect of Ostpolitik — a significant Soviet intelligence success.

subheadings.label: Atomic secrets and the Manhattan Project
facts: Klaus Fuchs passed detailed atomic weapons designs to the Soviets while working on the Manhattan Project — his intelligence accelerated the Soviet bomb programme by years. The Rosenbergs (executed 1953) passed related intelligence and became Cold War martyrs in the USA, inflaming McCarthyism.

The Baruch Plan (1946) — proposing international control of atomic weapons — was partly rejected by the USSR because they already knew, via Fuchs, that they could build their own bomb. Soviet espionage thus shaped the arms control debate.

subheadings.label: The Cambridge Five
facts: Kim Philby, Guy Burgess, Donald Maclean, Anthony Blunt and John Cairncross were recruited at Cambridge in the 1930s and passed intelligence to the Soviets for decades. Philby was particularly damaging as head of MI6's anti-Soviet section — he alerted the Soviets to operations against them and destroyed Western spy networks in the Eastern bloc.

The discovery of the Cambridge Five severely damaged Anglo-American intelligence cooperation. Philby fled to Moscow in 1963. Blunt was secretly pardoned by the British government in 1964 — his role was not publicly admitted until 1979.

subheadings.label: Later espionage
facts: Aldrich Ames (arrested 1994) was the most damaging CIA mole — he exposed virtually every Soviet agent working for the CIA, motivated by money. The U-2 incident (1960) showed how spy flights directly destroyed diplomacy — Khrushchev walked out of the Paris Summit after Eisenhower refused to apologise.

Gunter Guillaume's exposure in 1974 brought down Willy Brandt — a significant Stasi success. Espionage was a permanent feature of Cold War relations, reflecting the fact that both sides viewed each other as fundamentally hostile regardless of periods of détente.

heading: The Czech Crisis 1968
summary: The Prague Spring of 1968 threatened Soviet control of Eastern Europe — crushed by invasion and triggering the Brezhnev Doctrine.
facts: Czechoslovakia had been a prosperous democracy before the Second World War. Under Soviet rule, discontent was high — the economy was run for the good of the Soviet Union rather than for the Czechs; there was no freedom of speech; radio, newspapers and television were heavily censored. Antonin Novotny was a hard-line Communist who ruled using the secret police.

In 1968 Alexander Dubcek became head of Czechoslovakia. He introduced the Prague Spring — reforms aimed at creating Socialism with a human face: allowing some foreign travel, releasing political prisoners, relaxing censorship. Dubcek invited Tito of Yugoslavia for talks, which alarmed Brezhnev.

August 1968: the USSR, Poland, Hungary, Bulgaria and East Germany invaded Czechoslovakia with 500,000 troops. Dubcek was captured by Soviet paratroopers, taken to Moscow and encouraged to abandon his reforms. 150 Czechoslovak civilians were killed in resistance. Jan Palach set himself on fire in protest. Hard-line communist Gustav Husak replaced Dubcek.

Brezhnev issued the Brezhnev Doctrine to justify the invasion — if any communist country shows signs of turning towards capitalism it is the responsibility of all communist countries to force it back to communism. This was a direct threat to all other communist countries.

America failed to help — too busy with Vietnam. This again showed the West would not intervene in the Soviet sphere. Albania left the Warsaw Pact in protest. The Yugoslav and Romanian governments condemned the invasion and fostered closer links with China. Western communist parties cut ties with the USSR in protest.

subheadings.label: Causes
facts: Czechoslovakia had been a prosperous democracy before WWII. Under Soviet rule, discontent was high — the economy was run for the good of the USSR rather than Czechoslovakia; there was no freedom of speech; there were purges between 1949 and 1954. By the 1960s the Czech economy was in serious decline.

In January 1968, Alexander Dubček became leader of the Czech Communist Party and launched the 'Prague Spring' — a programme of liberalisation including freedom of speech, freedom of the press, freedom of movement and multi-party democracy. He called it 'socialism with a human face'.

subheadings.label: Events
facts: The USSR was alarmed — if the Czechs could liberalise, other satellite states would follow. Brezhnev warned Dubček repeatedly but Dubček refused to abandon his reforms. The Czechs argued they had the right to determine their own path to socialism.

In August 1968 the USSR, Poland, Hungary, Bulgaria and East Germany invaded Czechoslovakia with 500,000 troops. Dubček was captured by Soviet paratroopers, taken to Moscow and 'encouraged' to abandon his reforms. 150 Czechoslovak civilians were killed in resistance. Jan Palach set himself on fire in protest. Hard-line Gustáv Husák replaced Dubček.

subheadings.label: Consequences
facts: Consequences: America failed to help — too distracted by Vietnam. Albania left the Warsaw Pact in protest. Yugoslavia and Romania condemned the invasion and began to foster closer links with China. Western communist parties cut ties with the USSR in protest. The invasion weakened Soviet control of Eastern Europe in the long run.

heading: The Brezhnev Doctrine
summary: The Brezhnev Doctrine asserted the USSR's right to intervene in any communist country showing signs of turning towards capitalism — the ideological justification for Soviet imperialism.
facts: The Brezhnev Doctrine was issued in September 1968 to justify the Soviet invasion of Czechoslovakia. It stated that if any communist country showed signs of turning towards capitalism it was the responsibility of all communist countries to force it back to communism.

The Doctrine effectively ended the hopes raised by de-Stalinisation that Eastern European countries could develop their own national paths to socialism. It confirmed that the USSR would use military force to maintain Soviet control of the Eastern bloc.

The Doctrine was used to justify Soviet intervention in Afghanistan in 1979 — Brezhnev feared the Afghan communist government might fall to the Mujahedeen, setting a dangerous precedent on the USSR's southern border.

The significance of the Brezhnev Doctrine became clear only when Gorbachev abandoned it in 1988, replacing it with the Sinatra Doctrine — allowing satellite states to go their own way. Without the threat of Soviet military intervention, the communist regimes of Eastern Europe collapsed within a year.

The contrast between the Brezhnev Doctrine and the Sinatra Doctrine is central to understanding the end of the Cold War — it was Gorbachev's decision not to intervene militarily that allowed the revolutions of 1989 to succeed.

subheadings.label: What it stated
facts: Following the invasion of Czechoslovakia in August 1968, Brezhnev issued his doctrine to justify the intervention: if any communist country was showing signs of turning towards capitalism, it was the responsibility of all communist countries to force it back to communism.

The doctrine asserted the concept of 'limited sovereignty' — communist states were not fully sovereign if their actions threatened the socialist bloc as a whole. This directly contradicted the UN Charter's principle of national self-determination.

subheadings.label: Why it mattered
facts: In practice, the Brezhnev Doctrine meant that any satellite state attempting to leave the Warsaw Pact or adopt a multi-party system would face Soviet military intervention — as Hungary had in 1956 and Czechoslovakia in 1968.
The Doctrine cast a long shadow over Eastern Europe. It made clear to reformers in Poland, Hungary and Czechoslovakia that there were firm limits to how far they could challenge Soviet authority.

subheadings.label: The Sinatra Doctrine contrast
facts: Western communist parties were appalled — many cut ties with the USSR in protest at the invasion of Czechoslovakia. This process, known as 'Eurocommunism', saw Western communist parties increasingly distance themselves from Moscow.

Gorbachev replaced the Brezhnev Doctrine with the 'Sinatra Doctrine' in 1988 — satellite states were now free to 'do it their way'. This was the single most important decision enabling the 1989 revolutions, as it removed the threat of Soviet military intervention.

heading: Solidarity in Poland 1980–81
summary: The Solidarity movement in Poland was the most serious challenge to Soviet-bloc communist authority since Hungary in 1956 — contained by martial law rather than Soviet invasion.
facts: In 1980 workers at the Lenin Shipyard in Gdansk went on strike over food prices and working conditions. Led by Lech Walesa, they formed Solidarity — the first independent trade union in the Eastern bloc. Solidarity quickly grew to 10 million members.

Solidarity demanded not just better wages but free trade unions, the right to strike, freedom of speech and the release of political prisoners. It became a broad political movement threatening the communist government's monopoly on power.

The USSR was deeply alarmed. Brezhnev considered military intervention but ultimately decided against a repeat of Hungary or Czechoslovakia. Instead Soviet pressure forced the Polish communist government to act.
In December 1981 General Jaruzelski declared martial law in Poland. Solidarity was banned, Walesa and other leaders were imprisoned. The movement was driven underground but not destroyed.

The long-term significance of Solidarity was enormous. It had shown that communist rule could be challenged through mass popular organisation. Solidarity survived underground and in 1989, when Gorbachev dropped the Brezhnev Doctrine, it won the first free elections in Poland — becoming the first Eastern European country to abandon communism.

subheadings.label: The movement
facts: Economic unrest — including strikes in the Gdansk shipyards in 1980 — led the Polish government to recognise the Solidarity trade union movement. Solidarity, led by Lech Walesa, was the first independent trade union in the Eastern bloc.

In April 1981 the Round Table Agreements saw Solidarity recognised as a political party. There was to be a new constitution, with Solidarity allowed to compete with the Communist Party for 35% of the seats in a lower house of parliament. There would be free elections for the second chamber.

subheadings.label: Suppression
facts: However the USSR viewed Solidarity with deep alarm. A non-communist government in Poland would be unacceptable. Brezhnev threatened intervention. The Polish Communist Party leader Jaruzelski declared martial law in December 1981, suspending Solidarity and arresting its leaders including Walesa.

The elections of June 1981 resulted in a Solidarity government with some Communists holding major posts. The existing leader, Jaruzelski, remained president and Communists held key posts in the new government.

subheadings.label: Long-term significance
facts: Poland remained part of the Warsaw Pact but the USSR had accepted a non-Communist government and important constitutional change. This was a landmark — the first time the USSR had allowed a satellite state to move significantly away from communist one-party rule.

The role of Pope John Paul II — a Pole elected in 1979 — was crucial. His visits to Poland strengthened the resolve of the Polish people. The Catholic Church provided an alternative source of authority and community to the communist state.

heading: Détente and SALT
summary: Détente — the period of improved relations from 1969 to 1979 — produced landmark arms limitation agreements but ultimately failed to resolve the fundamental tensions of the Cold War.
facts: By the 1970s both superpowers had reasons to want to improve relations. The long-running arms race was expensive and the risk of MAD was real. The USSR was experiencing poor living standards. The USA was experiencing political problems at home and an expensive war in Vietnam. 40% of the Soviet economy was spent on nuclear weapons.

MIRVs (Multiple Independently Targeted Re-entry Vehicles, 1964 onwards): one of the most significant arms race developments of the 1960s — a single missile could now carry multiple warheads each aimed at different targets. MIRVs made the missile-launcher limits of SALT I partly illusory: both sides could increase their destructive capacity simply by adding warheads to existing missiles. The development of MIRVs drove continued escalation even during the period of détente.

The Outer Space Treaty (1967): signed by the USA, USSR and UK, banning nuclear weapons in space and prohibiting military bases on the moon. Part of a broader pattern of arms control agreements alongside the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty (1968) and the Partial Test Ban Treaty (1963) — but, like them, it addressed the form of escalation rather than reversing its substance.

SALT I (1972): President Nixon and Brezhnev signed the Strategic Arms Limitation Treaty. It restricted the number of ICBMs and SLBMs (submarine-launched ballistic missiles) each side could have. It did not include agreements on the most up-to-date weapons or clauses to get rid of current weapons. However it showed both sides were willing to negotiate.

In 1975, 35 nations from NATO and the Warsaw Pact signed the Helsinki Accords, agreeing on three main areas: European borders, scientific and trade co-operation, and human rights. Some US politicians were angered — the agreements on European borders appeared to accept Soviet control of Eastern Europe. There was also no way to enforce the human rights clauses.
The new spirit of co-operation was symbolised by the Apollo-Soyuz mission of 1975 — American astronauts and Soviet cosmonauts shaking hands in orbit, ending the Space Race.

In 1979 the USA and USSR tried to create SALT 2, putting more limitations on nuclear weapons. However SALT 2 was never signed because the USSR invaded Afghanistan in December 1979 and President Carter cancelled the treaty, ending détente.

subheadings.label: Why détente developed
facts: Détente is the term used for the period of improved relations between the USA and USSR from 1969 to 1980. Its roots lay in the Cuban Missile Crisis — both sides had come so close to nuclear war that they recognised the need for greater communication and arms control.

Reasons for détente: the USSR faced worsening relations with China — there were serious border clashes in 1969 and the USSR secretly asked the USA's reaction to a joint action against China's nuclear installations. The USA faced the costly Vietnam War and the sudden rise in oil prices in 1973. Both sides recognised that arms reduction would help their economies.

subheadings.label: What was achieved
facts: SALT I (1972): the Strategic Arms Limitation Talks established a 5-year freeze on constructing missile launchers and a freeze on ICBMs and submarine-launched ballistic missiles. Both sides agreed to restrict anti-ballistic screens to their capital cities and main missile sites. Nixon and Brezhnev visited each other in 1972/3.

Helsinki Accords (1975): 33 nations from NATO and the Warsaw Pact met. Three 'baskets' were agreed: Basket 1 — European borders are inviolable; Basket 2 — economic and scientific co-operation; Basket 3 — human rights are to be respected. Later that year, the Apollo-Soyuz Mission followed up the spirit of Basket 2.

SALT II (1979): proposed new treaty with greater bans on strategic bombers and ICBMs. Talks stalled and were eventually cancelled by President Carter due to growing distrust of the Soviet government, the Iranian Revolution of 1979, and the Soviet invasion of Afghanistan.

subheadings.label: Limitations and collapse
facts: In practice détente was 'just a piece of paper' — both sides still had enough nuclear weapons to initiate MAD. The human rights provisions of Helsinki were regularly ignored by the USSR. But it symbolised improving relations and reduced the immediate risk of nuclear confrontation.

heading: Ostpolitik
summary: Willy Brandt's Ostpolitik transformed West Germany's relationship with the Eastern bloc, normalising relations and reducing Cold War tensions in Europe.
facts: Ostpolitik (Eastern politics) was a policy of co-operation between West Germany and the Eastern Bloc in the late 1960s and early 1970s. It was pioneered by Willy Brandt, who became Chancellor of West Germany in 1969.

The Hallstein Doctrine had previously stated that recognising East Germany was an unfriendly act — West Germany refused to have diplomatic relations with any country that recognised the GDR. Brandt abandoned this.

Key achievements of Ostpolitik: the Basic Treaty of 1972 — East and West Germany recognised each other and both joined the UN; the Moscow Treaty (1970) — West Germany recognised the post-war borders of the USSR; the Warsaw Treaty (1970) — West Germany recognised the Oder-Neisse border with Poland.

Brandt won the Nobel Peace Prize in 1971 for his work. However Ostpolitik caused considerable controversy in West Germany — many felt it gave too much legitimacy to East Germany and the Soviet-imposed borders.

In 1974 Brandt was forced to resign when it was discovered his aide Gunter Guillaume was a spy for the East German Stasi. Despite this, Ostpolitik's achievements in normalising relations between the two Germanys and recognising borders were maintained by subsequent German governments.

subheadings.label: Background
facts: Ostpolitik (literally 'East Politics') was pursued by West German Chancellor Willy Brandt from 1969. The FRG Hallstein Doctrine had stated that West Germany would break off diplomatic relations with any state that officially recognised the DDR. Brandt saw this as unsustainable — Germany could not be so relentlessly divided.

subheadings.label: Key treaties
facts: Brandt signed the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty in 1969. He then began a series of complex treaties with the USSR, Poland, Czechoslovakia and the DDR.

The Moscow Treaty (August 1970) between Brandt and Brezhnev: neither had any territorial claim against any other state; it recognised the western frontier of Poland; Germany finally accepted the loss of territory of 1945 as 'inviolable'; the Federal Republic abandoned the Hallstein Doctrine and agreed both Germanies would become members of the UN.

A treaty with Poland was signed in December 1970 — ethnic Germans still in Poland were to be allowed to emigrate to the West and there were to be more trade links. A treaty with Czechoslovakia was signed in 1973, formally revoking the 1938 Munich Treaty. The Basic Treaty (December 1972) saw the FRG recognise the DDR as an equal sovereign state.

subheadings.label: Results
facts: In September 1971, it was agreed that there should be no restrictions on travel between the Federal Republic and West Berlin, and that West Berliners had a right to visit East Berlin.

Brandt won the Nobel Peace Prize in 1971. Ostpolitik gained concessions for West Berlin and had not weakened its ties with the USA or NATO. The way was left open for some future reunification — which came in 1990. However the DDR had gained recognition of its frontiers and there was no suggestion that the internal policies of the DDR should change.

heading: The Soviet invasion of Afghanistan
summary: The Soviet invasion of Afghanistan in December 1979 ended détente and began a costly ten-year war that exposed the weaknesses of the Red Army.
facts: In 1978 a communist revolutionary party (PDPA) had seized power in Afghanistan. Many Afghans rejected the communist government because its atheism was at odds with their Muslim faith — the communists imprisoned, tortured and murdered many Muslim religious leaders. This led to the formation of an anti-communist resistance movement known as the Mujahedeen.

To support the communists, Brezhnev invaded on Christmas Day 1979, beginning a 10-year war against the Mujahedeen. The Red Army was ill-prepared for the Afghan landscape. The Mujahedeen fought an effective guerrilla war. The Soviets killed the unpopular Afghan leader Amin and replaced him with the still unpopular but more pro-Moscow Kamal.

America was alarmed at Soviet involvement near the Persian Gulf — a major supplier of US oil. Carter supplied the Mujahedeen and issued the Carter Doctrine, stating that America would respond strongly to any attempts to take control of the Persian Gulf. The CIA funded Operation Cyclone, arming and training Mujahedeen fighters.

Détente ended: Carter scrapped SALT 2 and imposed economic sanctions including an end to the grain trade. America boycotted the 1980 Moscow Olympics (joined by 60 other countries). The USSR boycotted the 1984 Los Angeles Olympics in retaliation.

The USSR spent a total of $50 billion in Afghanistan (estimated). Cuba and Vietnam were receiving $1 billion of aid per year from the USSR by 1980. The financial strain of Afghanistan combined with other pressures contributed directly to the economic crisis that would eventually force Gorbachev's reforms.

subheadings.label: Why invaded
facts: In 1978 a communist revolutionary party (the PDPA) had seized power in Afghanistan. Many Afghans rejected the communist government because its atheism was at odds with their Muslim faith — the communists imprisoned, tortured and murdered many Muslim religious leaders. This led to the formation of an anti-communist resistance movement known as the Mujahedeen.

To support the communists, Brezhnev invaded Afghanistan on Christmas Day 1979 with 100,000 Soviet forces. They faced opposition inspired by Islamic beliefs and supported by the USA via Pakistan. Soviet troops withdrew in 1989 after a 10-year war.

subheadings.label: The war
facts: The problems of the war: the terrain led to a sustained guerrilla war echoing the US struggle in Vietnam. The opposition fighters had the support of local populations. The war damaged the reputation of the USSR not only in the West but also within the Soviet bloc — over 38,000 Soviets died or were wounded.

The war eroded the confidence of Soviet leaders in using military intervention. Previously, armed Soviet intervention in satellite states had been effective and short-lived. Afghanistan showed this was not always true — and military action was not seen as a viable option in 1989 when the Soviet Empire began to disintegrate.

subheadings.label: Consequences
facts: The war also weakened the Red Army's reputation — its inability to defeat guerrilla forces, the increasing resort to brutality, and the disintegration of discipline and morale combined to undermine the assumption of a great Soviet military machine capable of invading Europe.

The losses in Afghanistan increased resentment within the USSR from non-Russians, who felt they were paying the price for involvement in a war that brought little benefit outside Russia. Protests about the call-up of troops from the Baltic republics grew. 'Draft dodging' became common. When glasnost allowed press freedom, the reporting of the war brought about discontent and demand for political change.

heading: The new Cold War 1979–1984
summary: Reagan's military build-up and the breakdown of détente created a new period of intense superpower hostility after 1979.
facts: Carter lost the 1980 election for appearing too soft on the Soviets. Ronald Reagan was elected promising to be tough on the Soviets — beginning the Second Cold War. Reagan took a far tougher stance than any of his predecessors.

Reagan's rhetoric: he described the USSR as an evil empire, the focus of evil in the modern world, a totalitarian darkness, and compared them to the Nazis. He issued the Reagan Doctrine — the US would fund and support anti-communist resistance groups in communist countries. He also invaded Grenada in 1983 to topple the communist regime there.

Military spending: Reagan raised military spending to $1 Trillion. In 1983 he announced the Strategic Defence Initiative (SDI) or Star Wars — an orbital laser system to undermine MAD by shooting down Soviet missiles. The technology was not ready but Reagan announced it as if it was. This terrified the USSR as they were in no position to compete in their current economic state.

SDI was a turning point — it led Gorbachev to the conclusion that the USSR could not win an arms race with America and that radical change was needed. The threat of SDI contributed directly to Gorbachev's rise to power and his willingness to negotiate.

The new Cold War showed that détente had been fragile and dependent on restraint from both sides. The combination of Afghanistan, Reagan's rhetoric and SDI created the most dangerous period of Cold War tension since the Cuban Missile Crisis.

subheadings.label: Reagan's policies
facts: America was alarmed at Soviet involvement near the Persian Gulf (threatening US oil interests). President Carter issued the Carter Doctrine — stating that America would respond strongly to any attempts to take control of the Persian Gulf. Carter supplied the Mujahedeen via Pakistan with arms and money.

Economic sanctions on the USSR followed the Afghanistan invasion — Carter ended the US grain trade with the USSR. America refused to attend the 1980 Moscow Olympics; in retaliation the USSR refused to attend the 1984 Los Angeles Olympics.

Ronald Reagan took office in January 1981 with a far more aggressive anti-Soviet stance. He described the USSR as an 'evil empire' and dramatically increased US military spending — raising defence spending from $171 billion in 1981 to $376 billion in 1986.

subheadings.label: Soviet response
facts: Reagan developed the Strategic Defence Initiative (SDI — 'Star Wars') in 1983 — a space-based laser defence system designed to intercept Soviet ICBMs. This threatened to make all Soviet nuclear missiles obsolete, and the USSR could not afford to develop a comparable system.

subheadings.label: Assessment
facts: Reagan also stationed Pershing and Cruise missiles in Western Europe in 1983 in response to Soviet SS-20 missiles — causing widespread anti-nuclear protests across Western Europe (the 'peace movement').

The new Cold War was characterised by intense mutual suspicion — in 1983 the USSR shot down a South Korean airliner (KAL 007) that had strayed into Soviet airspace, killing all 269 people on board. Later that year, a Soviet nuclear early warning system falsely detected an American missile attack — the duty officer Stanislav Petrov's decision not to report it may have prevented nuclear war.

unit: Chapter 4 – The End of the Cold War 1984–1995
heading: Problems facing the USSR in the 1980s
summary: By the mid-1980s the USSR faced a deep structural economic crisis compounded by the costs of the arms race, Afghanistan and the Chernobyl disaster.
facts: Brezhnev's rule had been marked by the era of stagnation. The Soviet economy was failing — despite having 75% more farm land than the USA, the USSR produced less than 2/3 of the food. Collectivisation had caused food shortages in Czechoslovakia, East Germany and Hungary — food production was lower than it had been in 1938. Wages did not rise in pace with inflation, leading to worker discontent.

Military overstretch: a quarter of Soviet GDP was spent on the military. The USSR spent a total of $50 billion in Afghanistan with no results. Cuba and Vietnam were receiving $1 billion of aid per year by 1980. East Germany was forced to take Western aid to survive and by 1981 owed Western banks $12.8 billion.

Political stagnation: Brezhnev had been succeeded by the senile and ill Andropov and Chernenko who both died quickly and achieved little. Eastern bloc economies were struggling due to lack of technical innovation. Alcoholism was a common feature of life in the USSR and Eastern bloc, leading to social problems.

In 1986 the Chernobyl nuclear meltdown cost $18 billion in containment. Ronald Reagan's Star Wars programme had reignited the costly arms and space race. The CIA funded Operation Cyclone, arming and training Mujahedeen fighters in Afghanistan from 1979.

In 1989 men from non-Russian Soviet republics like Georgia refused conscription, showing growing opposition to Soviet rule. Poor living standards and lack of human rights were causing unrest in satellite states — exemplified by Solidarity in Poland in 1981. Gorbachev became leader in 1985 — he realised radical change was needed to save the USSR.

subheadings.label: Economic problems
facts: Brezhnev's rule had been marked by the 'era of stagnation' — the Soviet economy was failing. The Soviet Union had tried to keep up with the USA in the arms race but could not afford to do so. Between 1970 and 1982 defence spending was 15-17% of GDP.
The war in Afghanistan was costing vast amounts of money with no results — over 38,000 Soviets died or were wounded. It eroded the confidence of Soviet leaders in using military intervention.

In 1986 the Chernobyl nuclear power station exploded — $18 billion was spent on containment. The disaster exposed the inefficiency and corruption of Soviet industry and the dangers of the Soviet economic system.

subheadings.label: Military overstretch
facts: Poor living standards and lack of human rights was causing unrest in the satellite states — for example Solidarity in Poland in 1981. The USSR's declining economy meant it could not meet the consumer demands of its own people or its satellite states.

The two elderly leaders who followed Brezhnev — Yuri Andropov and Konstantin Chernenko — had meant that stagnation characterised policy at a vital time. When Gorbachev became leader in 1985 at the relatively young age of 54, there was widespread understanding in party circles that severe economic problems existed and radical change was needed.

subheadings.label: Political stagnation
facts: The arms race was also a major factor — Reagan's Strategic Defence Initiative (Star Wars) threatened to make all Soviet ICBMs obsolete. The USSR could not afford to compete with this new technology. Its economy was stagnant and its technology had not kept up with that of the West.

unit: Chapter 4 – The End of the Cold War 1984–1995
heading: Gorbachev and the withdrawal from Afghanistan
summary: Gorbachev's decision to withdraw from Afghanistan was central to his New Thinking — and to the financial and political pressures that accelerated the end of the Cold War.
facts: When Gorbachev came to power in 1985 he inherited the Afghan war — already six years old with no prospect of victory. He described Afghanistan as a bleeding wound. The war was costing $8 billion a year and had killed over 15,000 Soviet soldiers. It was deeply unpopular at home.

The Red Army was ill-suited to fighting a guerrilla war in the Afghan mountains. The Mujahedeen were increasingly well-equipped — the CIA's Operation Cyclone was providing them with Stinger missiles capable of shooting down Soviet helicopters, which had been a key Soviet military advantage.

Gorbachev began reducing Soviet forces in Afghanistan as part of his New Thinking — he recognised that the USSR could not afford to maintain military commitments across the world whilst also reforming its economy at home. He also recognised that the war was damaging Soviet relations with the Muslim world.

The Geneva Accords of April 1988 — signed by Afghanistan, Pakistan, the USSR and the USA — committed the USSR to withdrawing its forces. The last Soviet troops left Afghanistan in February 1989. The communist Afghan government survived until 1992.

The withdrawal from Afghanistan was significant for the Cold War in several ways: it showed Gorbachev was serious about New Thinking and willing to accept a strategic retreat; it removed one of the major causes of the new Cold War and enabled arms negotiations with the West; and it demonstrated the limits of Soviet military power, undermining the USSR's superpower status.

unit: Chapter 4 – The End of the Cold War 1984–1995
heading: Gorbachev — perestroika and glasnost
summary: Gorbachev's twin reforms of perestroika and glasnost were intended to revitalise the USSR — but instead unleashed forces that would destroy it.
facts: Gorbachev became leader in 1985. Brezhnev's rule had been marked by the era of stagnation — the Soviet economy was failing, huge amounts of money were being sucked into Afghanistan with no results, the 1986 Chernobyl nuclear meltdown had cost $18 billion, and poor living standards were causing unrest in satellite states. Gorbachev realised radical change was needed to save the USSR and introduced New Thinking.

Perestroika (Restructuring): the restructuring of the Soviet economy. Individuals and foreigners could now invest in businesses — up to 49% of a Soviet business. Soviet state retained control of key industries. Designed to bring the failing Soviet economy up to the standard of the West by introducing some elements of a market economy.

Glasnost (Openness): greater freedom of speech and the press. Political prisoners were released. Soviet citizens were openly encouraged to discuss and seek solutions to the problems facing the USSR. The result was an unstoppable wave of criticism of the system.

In December 1988 Gorbachev made a speech to the United Nations in New York where he announced he would drop the Brezhnev Doctrine and withdraw half a million Red Army troops from Eastern Europe. This became known as the Sinatra Doctrine — satellite states were now free to do it their own way. Aimed at easing Soviet military spending but severely undermined Soviet control in Europe.

Reagan felt like he could work with Gorbachev. From 1985 there were a series of summits: Washington 1987 — Intermediate Range Nuclear Force (INF) Treaty, a major arms reduction; Malta 1989 — Gorbachev and Reagan's successor George Bush Snr announced the end of the Cold War.

subheadings.label: Perestroika
facts: Perestroika ('restructuring') referred to the restructuring of the economy — relaxing centralised control and permitting greater economic freedom and initiative. In June 1987, private enterprise was allowed in some industries. However the changes did not lead to grateful appreciation — new private industries did not all prove efficient and long-term economic problems continued. There were more shortages than before of some goods.

subheadings.label: Glasnost
facts: Glasnost ('openness') was an 'openness' that would allow more discussion of economic and political issues to drive progress. In 1986 state controls of the media were relaxed and the public learnt about the inefficiencies and corruption that had come to characterise national and local political and economic management.

subheadings.label: Political change
facts: Political change: in January 1987 Gorbachev spoke openly to the Central Committee of the weaknesses of the system and proposed much greater public participation. Multi-candidate elections by secret ballot for local councils were proposed. In February 1989 there were elections for a new Congress of People's Deputies, which saw the defeat of many of the party establishment. New political leaders from outside the party emerged — including Boris Yeltsin.

subheadings.label: The Sinatra Doctrine
facts: The Sinatra Doctrine (1988): Gorbachev replaced the Brezhnev Doctrine with the 'Sinatra Doctrine' — satellite states were now free to 'do it their way'. This was aimed at easing Soviet military spending and avoiding hypocrisy but severely undermined Soviet control in Europe.

The changes divided the Communist Party. Some hardliners felt this was a dangerous path — the threat from the USA and China was unresolved. Others wanted more radical reforms. The hold of the Communist Party began to weaken and new political organisations began to form.

By 1989, Gorbachev would not bolster unpopular communist regimes that were unwilling to apply the remedies he had introduced in the USSR. Thus, integral changes in the USSR paved the way for a new détente — and meant that instead of pressure for change being dictated by Western pressure, it was coming from the leadership of the USSR itself.

unit: Chapter 4 – The End of the Cold War 1984–1995
heading: Reagan, the arms race and Western pressure
summary: Reagan's aggressive military build-up and Strategic Defence Initiative put enormous pressure on the USSR's already failing economy — though Gorbachev's internal reforms were equally important in ending the Cold War.
facts: Reagan took a far tougher stance on the USSR than his predecessors. He described them as an evil empire, the focus of evil in the modern world, and compared them to the Nazis. He issued the Reagan Doctrine — the US would fund and support anti-communist resistance groups in communist countries.

Reagan raised military spending to $1 Trillion. In 1983 he announced the Strategic Defence Initiative (SDI) or Star Wars — an orbital laser system to undermine MAD. The technology was not ready but Reagan announced it as if it was. This terrified the USSR as they were in no position to compete economically and led to Gorbachev's rise.

The limitations of Western pressure: the USA did not intervene militarily in Eastern Europe — not in Poland in 1981, and not when the Berlin Wall was built in 1961. Containment was the policy, not rollback. Reagan's rhetoric was aggressive but stopped short of direct military confrontation.

The CIA funded Operation Cyclone, arming and training Mujahedeen fighters in Afghanistan from 1979 — contributing to the costly Soviet defeat there. Economic sanctions and the Olympic boycotts imposed costs on the USSR but did not fundamentally change Soviet behaviour.

Ultimately Reagan and Gorbachev worked together to end the Cold War. Reagan felt he could work with Gorbachev — at the Washington Summit of 1987 they signed the INF Treaty destroying intermediate-range missiles. At Malta in 1989 Gorbachev and Bush announced the end of the Cold War.

subheadings.label: Reagan's actions
facts: The new Republican administration of Ronald Reagan was suspicious of the USSR and concerned about the Soviet invasion of Afghanistan and the expansion of Soviet naval forces. Reagan increased US military spending and extended the arms race. He rejected the previous restrictions on defence systems.

With the development of highly sophisticated and expensive new laser and space-based systems (the Strategic Defence Initiative — 'Star Wars'), there was the possibility that the USA could actually win a future conflict. This put the USSR at a disadvantage as its economy was stagnant and its technology had not kept up.

Reagan also fought communist influence in the developing world — supporting anti-communist forces in Nicaragua and invading Grenada. The aid to insurgents in Afghanistan, however, was more serious — it contributed to the Soviet decision that the war was unwinnable.

subheadings.label: Limitations of Western pressure
facts: However, the pressure of the arms race must be kept in perspective. Soviet military spending was already high and did not increase in response to the arms race. The problem was that economic growth was falling and there was a shortage of oil — it was this rather than just pressure from the West that led Gorbachev to seek a way to scale back the arms race.

Reagan and Gorbachev met at Reykjavik in 1986 — Gorbachev attempted to persuade Reagan to give up the SDI developments. Though this failed, Gorbachev succeeded in getting the total withdrawal of medium-range missiles in Europe at a conference between the USSR and NATO in Washington in 1987 — the INF Treaty.

subheadings.label: Outcomes
facts: The new détente of 1985–88 was an indication that the USSR was susceptible to pressure. It is possible that the main driving force was the internal situation in the USSR and its republics and satellites — but Western influence and the arms race were a contributory factor.

unit: Chapter 4 – The End of the Cold War 1984–1995
heading: The revolutions of 1989
summary: In 1989, communist regimes across Eastern Europe collapsed in rapid succession — the result of accumulated internal discontent, economic failure and Gorbachev's refusal to use force.
facts: Gorbachev's New Thinking in the USSR sparked unrest in Eastern Europe. People saw the greater freedoms Soviet citizens were enjoying and wanted the same. However their hard-line leaders like Erich Honecker in East Germany refused to reform. Without the threat of Soviet military intervention — Gorbachev had dropped the Brezhnev Doctrine — the communist regimes could not survive.

Poland led the way: Solidarity won 160 of 161 freely contested seats in the June 1989 elections — the communists were swept from power. When Gorbachev did not intervene, the other satellite states followed Poland's example.

Negotiated revolutions (countries where governments contemplated reform): Hungary opened its borders with Austria in 1989 — 150,000 East Germans fled West. Bulgaria's Communist Party removed its own leader and began reforms. In Czechoslovakia mass protests led to the Velvet Revolution — Vaclav Havel, who had spent the first 5 months of 1989 in prison, became President.

Resistance to change: East Germany — Erich Honecker tried to hold on but resigned in October 1989 after 70,000 protesters marched through Leipzig. Romania — the unpopular leader Ceausescu was executed on Christmas Day 1989.

By the end of 1989 all of Eastern Europe was capitalist. The revolutionary wave was best symbolised by the fall of the Berlin Wall on 9th November 1989 — East Germans demanding its fall and starting to knock it down.

subheadings.label: Common causes
facts: Common elements in the events of 1989: a build-up of resentment against a background of economic underperformance and rising prices; reforming leaders and groups ready to share power; acceptance by Gorbachev and Moscow that states outside the USSR should make changes; widespread popular support for change; rapid arrangements for free elections.

subheadings.label: Country by country
facts: Poland: economic unrest including strikes in the shipyards of Gdansk in 1988 led the government to recognise the Solidarity movement. In April 1989 Round Table Agreements saw Solidarity recognised as a political party. The elections of June 1989 resulted in a Solidarity government — the first non-communist government in Eastern Europe since 1948.

Hungary: unrest in 1988 resulted in the replacement of Kadar by a reforming communist. In 1989 Hungary agreed to hold free elections and opened its borders with Austria in August — this made it possible for 150,000 East Germans to leave for the West via this route.

The DDR: Hungary's open borders triggered demonstrations in Leipzig in September and October 1989. The East German leader Honecker could not count on Gorbachev — who advised him to make changes. The government allowed free exit from 10 November 1989 — and as soon as this was announced, border guards opened up crossing points from East to West Berlin, effectively opening the Berlin Wall. The Wall was subsequently torn down by crowds.

Czechoslovakia — the Velvet Revolution: news from Berlin led to large-scale demonstrations. Opposition groups including Charter 77, led by the dramatist Vaclav Havel, formed Civic Forum. In December a coalition government was formed in which communists were only a minority — Havel was made president. This led to the peaceful end of communism and the formation of Slovakia and the Czech Republic in 1992.

Romania: the only violent revolution. Demonstrations against President Ceausescu began in November 1989 — Ceausescu and his wife fled but were captured and executed on 25 December 1989 — the only leaders to suffer this fate.

unit: Chapter 4 – The End of the Cold War 1984–1995
heading: The fall of the Berlin Wall
summary: The fall of the Berlin Wall on 9 November 1989 was the defining moment of the end of the Cold War — a symbol of communist failure and the triumph of popular pressure.
facts: The fall of the Berlin Wall on 9th November 1989 was the result of a chain of events: Hungary had opened its borders with Austria allowing East Germans to flee West; mass protests had swept East Germany; Erich Honecker had resigned in October 1989.

On the evening of 9th November 1989 an East German spokesman announced that new travel regulations would allow East Germans to travel freely. The announcement was meant to be temporary and controlled — but was misunderstood as meaning the borders were open immediately. Thousands of East Germans gathered at the Wall checkpoints. The overwhelmed guards let them through.
East Germans poured through into West Berlin. German friends and families were reunited after 28 years. People began to knock down the Wall itself. The scenes were broadcast live around the world.

The fall of the Wall demonstrated the total loss of Soviet control as East Germans demanded its fall. It had been built in 1961 to stop people fleeing East Germany — its fall symbolised the complete failure of the communist system to deliver a life that people wanted to stay for.
Germany was reunified officially in October 1990. The fall of the Wall was the most powerful symbol of the end of the Cold War and the collapse of communist rule in Eastern Europe.

subheadings.label: Why it fell
facts: The Berlin Wall had been built in 1961 to stop the 'brain drain' of East Germans fleeing to the West. By 1989, Hungary's decision to open its borders with Austria had allowed 150,000 East Germans to leave via Hungary. This triggered growing demonstrations in East German cities, especially Leipzig.

The East German leader Honecker was unable to rely on Soviet support — Gorbachev had made clear he would not use force to maintain communist regimes. Honecker was replaced by the reforming communist Egon Krenz.

subheadings.label: The events
facts: On 9 November 1989 the government announced that East Germans would be allowed to travel freely. As soon as this was announced, border guards — overwhelmed by crowds — opened up crossing points. Crowds began demolishing the Wall with hammers and pickaxes. The Wall was subsequently torn down.

subheadings.label: Significance
facts: West German Chancellor Helmut Kohl moved rapidly to push for reunification. In March 1990 the first free elections were held in East Germany — the Alliance for Germany (pro-reunification) won a clear majority.

On 1 July 1990 the economies of the two Germanys became one — the first time in history that a capitalist and a socialist economy had suddenly become one. On 3 October 1990 Germany was formally reunified. The four wartime Allies formally recognised German reunification in the 'Two Plus Four Treaty'.

Reunification brought major problems: confusion about property rights (over 2 million claims filed); East German production costs were very high; links to the collapsing socialist economies of the Soviet Union and Eastern Europe meant East German factories could no longer sell their goods. Massive investment from West Germany was needed.

unit: Chapter 4 – The End of the Cold War 1984–1995
heading: German reunification
summary: German reunification on 3 October 1990 was the defining consequence of the Cold War's end in Europe — achieved rapidly but with enormous economic challenges.
facts: German reunification was achieved faster than almost anyone had anticipated. Following the fall of the Berlin Wall in November 1989, Chancellor Helmut Kohl of West Germany announced a Ten Point Plan for reunification in November 1989.
Free elections in East Germany in March 1990 resulted in a decisive victory for parties supporting rapid reunification. East Germany formally adopted the West German currency in July 1990.

The Two Plus Four Treaty (September 1990) settled the international aspects of reunification — the two Germanys plus the four wartime powers (USA, USSR, UK, France). The USSR agreed to accept reunification in exchange for a German commitment not to station NATO forces on former East German territory and significant West German financial aid.

West Germany formally absorbed East Germany on 3rd October 1990 — German Unity Day. The challenges were enormous: East Germany's economy was far weaker than the West's; huge investment was needed; many East Germans felt overwhelmed by the rapid changes.

German reunification was significant for the Cold War as it resolved the central European question that had dominated the conflict since 1945. A reunified Germany within NATO was exactly what the USSR had feared and tried to prevent — its acceptance by Gorbachev symbolised the end of Soviet power in Europe.

subheadings.label: How achieved
facts: German reunification (3 October 1990) was achieved with remarkable speed under Chancellor Helmut Kohl, who feared a window of opportunity might close. The 'Two Plus Four Treaty' — between the two Germanies and the four wartime Allies — formally recognised reunification and settled the borders of the new state.

On 1 July 1990 the economies of the two Germanies became one — the first time in history that a capitalist and a socialist economy had suddenly merged. The West German Deutschmark replaced the East German Mark at a 1:1 exchange rate, which was economically generous to East Germans but made East German industry instantly uncompetitive.

subheadings.label: Challenges
facts: Reunification brought major structural challenges: East German production costs were very high; links to the collapsing Soviet-bloc economies meant East German factories lost their markets overnight; massive confusion about property rights from successive waves of Nazi, Soviet and GDR expropriations meant over 2 million claims were filed by the December 1992 deadline.

West German investment in the East was enormous — hundreds of billions of Deutschmarks were transferred in the years after reunification. However unemployment in the East rose sharply as uncompetitive factories closed. Many East Germans felt like second-class citizens in the new unified Germany — a phenomenon described as the 'wall in the head'.

subheadings.label: Significance
facts: France and the USSR were initially unhappy about German reunification — both feared a powerful unified Germany. Gorbachev eventually agreed in return for assurances that NATO would not expand eastwards beyond Germany — an assurance that would become highly controversial in later decades.

Reunification was undoubtedly a triumph for West German diplomacy and for the West's Cold War strategy. It was also a vindication of the Ostpolitik pursued by Willy Brandt — the patient normalisation of relations with the East had laid the groundwork for the peaceful unification that followed.

unit: Chapter 4 – The End of the Cold War 1984–1995
heading: The coup of 1991 and collapse of the USSR
summary: Gorbachev's reforms had unleashed forces — nationalist movements in Soviet republics and hardline communist opposition — that culminated in a coup attempt and the final collapse of the USSR.
facts: Whilst Gorbachev was seen as a hero in the West (awarded the Nobel Peace Prize in 1990), in the USSR he was seen as weak. The constituent republics of the USSR saw how easily the satellite states had gained their independence and began to demand the same. In 1990 Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania declared independence.

Other constituent republics began to follow, including Russia — the largest republic — led by its president Boris Yeltsin in early 1991. Gorbachev proposed a voluntary Union Treaty in April 1991 to try to prevent the collapse of the USSR.

In August 1991 eight Communist leaders organised a coup and removed Gorbachev from power. They removed Glasnost and Perestroika. However Boris Yeltsin led the resistance — standing on a tank outside the Russian parliament — and overthrew the coup after just three days, restoring Gorbachev to power.

The affair demonstrated how little power Gorbachev now had. Yeltsin acted like he was in control and Gorbachev was just his puppet. Christmas Day 1991 — to avoid a civil war — Gorbachev resigned and announced the breakup of the USSR.
Yeltsin became the first president of Russia, turning it capitalist. The USSR was formally dissolved on 25th December 1991.

subheadings.label: The coup
facts: Whilst Gorbachev was seen as a hero in the West (awarded the Nobel Peace Prize in 1990), in the USSR he was seen as weak. The constituent republics of the USSR saw how easily the satellite states had gained their independence and began to demand the same.
In 1990, Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania declared independence from the USSR. Other constituent republics began to follow suit — including Russia, the largest republic, led by Boris Yeltsin.

Gorbachev was increasingly unpopular in Moscow, especially amongst hard-line Communists. In August 1991 eight communist leaders organised a coup and removed Gorbachev from power. They removed glasnost and perestroika.

subheadings.label: Why it failed
facts: However Boris Yeltsin led the resistance — standing on a tank outside the Russian Parliament, he rallied popular opposition to the coup. The coup collapsed after just 3 days, restoring Gorbachev to power. But the affair demonstrated how little power Gorbachev had now — Yeltsin acted like he was in control and Gorbachev was just his puppet.

subheadings.label: Consequences
facts: Christmas Day 1991: to avoid a civil war, Gorbachev resigned and announced the breakup of the USSR. The Soviet flag was lowered over the Kremlin and replaced by the Russian flag. Yeltsin became the 1st president of Russia — turning it capitalist.

unit: Chapter 4 – The End of the Cold War 1984–1995
heading: Russia under Yeltsin
summary: Boris Yeltsin's Russia faced enormous challenges in transitioning from communism to capitalism — economic chaos, political instability and the loss of superpower status.
facts: Yeltsin introduced economic shock therapy — an attempt to quickly transform the planned Soviet economy into a market economy. Its main steps were price liberalisation, an end to subsidies and stabilisation of the budget deficit.

In theory reforms should have quickly converted Russia into a market economy. In practice they were executed only in part. Prices were liberalised at the start of 1992, which led to massive inflation and the devaluation of savings — but also to goods appearing in stores for the first time.

The gross national product dropped by almost 40% between 1989 and 1995 according to official statistics. Soviet enterprises continued to produce goods that could not be sold and which no one needed. Most members of the Supreme Council were not convinced reforms were necessary.

Political instability: in 1993 Yeltsin faced a constitutional crisis when he ordered parliament to dissolve — it refused and supporters barricaded themselves inside. Yeltsin ordered tanks to fire on the parliament building. Russia held new elections in December 1993.

Yeltsin's Russia was marked by the rise of the oligarchs — a small group of businessmen who acquired vast wealth by buying state assets cheaply during privatisation. Corruption was widespread. Despite the chaos, Russia remained a democracy and held elections, and Yeltsin was re-elected in 1996.

subheadings.label: Economic shock therapy
facts: Boris Yeltsin became the first president of the Russian Federation after Gorbachev resigned on Christmas Day 1991. He had been elected president of Russia in June 1991 with 57% of the vote — the first democratic election in Russian history.

Yeltsin introduced 'shock therapy' — a rapid transition to a market economy. Price controls were removed overnight in January 1992, causing hyperinflation. The rouble lost most of its value. Many Russians saw their savings wiped out and living standards collapse.

subheadings.label: Political instability
facts: State industries were privatised rapidly — but the process was corrupt. A small group of well-connected businessmen (the 'oligarchs') acquired vast state assets at far below their true value, becoming billionaires overnight while ordinary Russians suffered.

Yeltsin faced political instability at home. In October 1993, hard-line communist opponents of reform barricaded themselves in the Russian parliament (the 'White House'). Yeltsin ordered tanks to shell the building — at least 187 people were killed. This was the most violent political confrontation in Moscow since the Bolshevik Revolution.

subheadings.label: Assessment
facts: In December 1994 Yeltsin launched a military campaign to prevent the breakaway republic of Chechnya from gaining independence. Russian forces suffered humiliating defeats against Chechen guerrillas. The war cost thousands of lives and further damaged Yeltsin's reputation.

By the mid-1990s Yeltsin's health was failing and his public appearances were frequently embarrassing. Russia had lost its superpower status, its economy was in crisis, and its international influence was a fraction of the USSR's. Yeltsin resigned on 31 December 1999, handing power to his chosen successor — Vladimir Putin.

unit: Chapter 4 – The End of the Cold War 1984–1995
heading: The collapse of Yugoslavia
summary: Yugoslavia's collapse into civil war after communism's fall showed how ethnic and religious tensions suppressed by communist rule could produce catastrophic violence.
facts: Yugoslavia had been a communist country under Tito that had maintained independence from the USSR. After Tito's death in 1980 Yugoslavia was held together with increasing difficulty. It was a multi-ethnic state with deep divisions between Serbs, Croats, Bosniaks, Slovenes, Albanians and others.

When communism collapsed across Eastern Europe in 1989-91, Yugoslavia began to break apart. Slovenia and Croatia declared independence in June 1991. Serbian president Slobodan Milosevic invaded Croatia and Slovenia to try to prevent the breakup, beginning a series of brutal wars.

The Bosnian War (1992-95) was the most devastating. When Bosnia declared independence, Bosnian Serbs — backed by Milosevic — launched a campaign of ethnic cleansing against Bosniaks and Croats. The siege of Sarajevo lasted nearly 4 years. Around 100,000 people died.

The international response was slow and inadequate. The UN deployed peacekeepers but with a limited mandate. The worst atrocity was the Srebrenica massacre of 1995 when Bosnian Serb forces killed around 8,000 Bosniak men and boys under the eyes of Dutch UN peacekeepers.

The Dayton Accord signed in 1995 ended the Bosnian War, dividing Bosnia into two entities. NATO bombing had been crucial in forcing the Serbs to the negotiating table. Yugoslavia's collapse demonstrated that the end of the Cold War did not bring stability — nationalist conflicts suppressed under communism could now erupt with devastating consequences.

subheadings.label: Causes
facts: Yugoslavia had been a unique communist state — Tito had resisted Stalin and maintained independence. It was a federation of six republics and two autonomous regions with a complex ethnic and religious mix. Tito's death in 1980 removed the one figure who had held the federation together.

Serbian nationalist Slobodan Milosevic became president of Serbia in 1989 and promoted the interests of Serbs across Yugoslavia. This fuelled nationalist movements in Slovenia and Croatia, which declared independence in June 1991. War broke out immediately — the Yugoslav People's Army (largely Serbian-controlled) fought the breakaway republics.

subheadings.label: The wars
facts: In Bosnia, a three-way conflict between Bosnian Muslims, Bosnian Serbs and Bosnian Croats led to the worst violence in Europe since WWII. Serbian forces conducted 'ethnic cleansing' — massacring or expelling Bosnian Muslims from their homes. The Srebrenica massacre of July 1995 saw 8,000 Bosnian Muslim men and boys murdered.

The international community was slow to respond. The UN deployed peacekeepers who lacked the mandate to stop the killing. The USA and NATO eventually intervened — NATO bombing campaigns against Serb positions in Bosnia in 1995 forced the Dayton Peace Agreement.

subheadings.label: International response
facts: In Kosovo (1999), NATO launched a 78-day air campaign against Serbia after Milosevic launched a campaign of ethnic cleansing against Kosovar Albanians. Serbian forces withdrew from Kosovo, which remained technically part of Serbia under UN administration.

Religion mobilised ethnic elimination of minority groups — Orthodox Christianity, Catholicism and Islam all reinforced old stereotypes and nationalist identities. The Yugoslav wars showed the dangerous consequences of communism's fall in multi-ethnic states — when the communist framework suppressing ethnic nationalism was removed, old rivalries re-emerged with catastrophic force.
